restaurants.name: Murano
restaurants.whyGo: Angela Hartnett's Mayfair dining room, starred within four months of opening in 2008.
restaurants.opNote: Named after the Venetian glass-making island. Northern Italian cooking in a formal Mayfair room.

restaurants.name: Trullo
restaurants.address: 300-302 St Paul's Rd, London N1 2LH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Tim Siadatan (ex St John, Moro) cooking a frequently changing seasonal menu of hand-made pasta and charcoal-grilled meats.
restaurants.signature: Pappardelle with eight-hour beef shin ragu
restaurants.opNote: Highbury trattoria, long regarded as one of London's best neighbourhood Italians.

restaurants.name: Manteca
restaurants.whyGo: Chris Leach and David Carter's nose-to-tail Italian with hand-rolled pasta and a salumeria on site.
restaurants.opNote: Whole-animal butchery feeding a menu of house-cured salumi and hand-rolled pasta.

restaurants.name: Legare
restaurants.address: Cardamom Bldg, 31G Shad Thames, Tower Bridge, London SE1 2YR, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Opened 2019 by Jay Patel (ex Barrafina) and chef Matt Beardmore (ex Trullo), in the warehouse streets by Tower Bridge.
restaurants.opNote: Neighbourhood Italian in the historic Shad Thames warehouse quarter.

restaurants.name: Bocca di Lupo
restaurants.whyGo: Regional cooking from across the whole of Italy, served trattoria-style in a buzzy Soho room. Counter seats face the kitchen.
restaurants.opNote: Dishes labelled by region; small and large plate sizes of everything.

restaurants.name: Bancone
restaurants.address: 39 William IV St, London WC2N 4DD, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Watch the pasta being rolled at the counter, at prices well below the Michelin Guide average.

restaurants.name: Padella
restaurants.whyGo: A short menu of hand-rolled pasta at low prices, which is why the queue exists.
restaurants.opNote: Original site opened in Borough Market 2016; now also Shoreditch and Soho, where limited bookings are taken.

restaurants.name: Italian Greyhound
restaurants.whyGo: From the Open House Group founders; local-trattoria spirit in a more polished contemporary room.

restaurants.name: Brutto
restaurants.whyGo: Deliberately unfussy Florentine cooking; the bistecca is the order.

restaurants.name: Lina Stores
restaurants.whyGo: The mint-green Brewer Street deli since 1944, now with restaurants attached.
restaurants.opNote: Fresh pasta counter and deli; the restaurants came much later than the shop.

restaurants.name: Sparrow
restaurants.whyGo: Spaghetti with pistachio pesto, lobster linguine, spicy vodka rigatoni.

restaurants.name: River Café
restaurants.address: Thames Wharf, Rainville Rd, London W6 9HA, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Michelin-starred simplicity on the Thames, where Jamie Oliver and Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall both trained. The terrace tables are the ones everyone wants.
restaurants.opNote: Informal in atmosphere, upmarket in cooking; the riverside seats book furthest ahead.

restaurants.name: Cecconi's
restaurants.whyGo: Soho House group's all-day Mayfair room behind the Royal Academy - wraparound windows, striped marble, white-jacketed service.
restaurants.opNote: Serves through the day, from egg-white omelette to lobster spaghetti.

restaurants.name: Gloria
restaurants.address: 54-56 Great Eastern St, London EC2A 3QR, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Big Mamma group's deliberately over-the-top trattoria, with a menu that changes every month.

restaurants.name: Luca
restaurants.address: 88 St John St, London EC1M 4EH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Italian cooking through British produce, from the Clove Club team.

restaurants.name: Circolo Popolare
restaurants.whyGo: Big Mamma group's Fitzrovia room, wall-to-wall bottles and a ceiling of greenery. Booked out well ahead.

restaurants.name: Bon Vino
restaurants.whyGo: Neighbourhood Italian near London Bridge, picked out by TOPJAW alongside Flour & Grape.

restaurants.name: Flour & Grape
restaurants.whyGo: Bermondsey Street pasta-and-wine spot; short menu, low prices, long queues.

restaurants.name: Napoli on the Road
restaurants.address: 9A Devonshire Rd, Chiswick, London W4 2EU, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Named best pizzeria in Europe for the third year running. Michele Pascarella's Chiswick pizzeria, a long way from the tourist centre and worth the journey.
restaurants.opNote: Ranked #1 in Europe by 50 Top Pizza three consecutive years to 2026.

restaurants.name: 50 Kalò
restaurants.whyGo: Ciro Salvo's London outpost, fourth in Europe in the 2026 rankings and a rare high-end pizzeria in the middle of tourist London.
restaurants.opNote: Central location makes it the most reachable of the top-ranked pizzerias.

restaurants.name: L'Antica Pizzeria da Michele
restaurants.whyGo: The London arm of the Naples institution founded in 1870, 28th in Europe in 2026. A very short menu, done the Naples way.
restaurants.opNote: Naples-born chain; Baker Street is the branch named in the 2026 rankings.

restaurants.name: Connie's Pizza
restaurants.whyGo: Entered the European top 50 at 48 within a year of opening, and took the 'one to watch' award with it.
restaurants.opNote: Newest of the four London entries; location not yet confirmed - needs a check before publication.
restaurants.signals: 50 Top Pizza Europa - #48 in Europe, One to Watch

restaurants.name: Homeslice
restaurants.whyGo: Twenty-inch pizzas sold whole or by the slice, with toppings split across halves. Built for groups rather than couples.
restaurants.opNote: Multiple central branches; Neal's Yard is the original.

restaurants.name: Pizza Pilgrims
restaurants.whyGo: Started as a Soho market cart in 2012 and now runs across London. Seventh in the 50 Top World Artisan Pizza Chains list.
restaurants.opNote: Reliable rather than remarkable, but consistent across every branch and easy to walk into.

restaurants.name: Santa Maria
restaurants.whyGo: A small Ealing pizzeria that built its reputation on strict Neapolitan method before the current wave arrived.

restaurants.name: Zia Lucia
restaurants.whyGo: Offers four different doughs including a 48-hour and a charcoal base, which makes it the most useful of the group for gluten-sensitive diners.

restaurants.name: Franco Manca
restaurants.whyGo: Sourdough pizza at a price nothing else central matches, from an operation that began in Brixton Market in 2008.
restaurants.opNote: CONTRACTING: nine London branches confirmed closing in 2026, including the original Brixton Market site, plus Battersea, Broadway Market and Stoke Newington. Check the specific branch is trading before recommending it.

restaurants.name: La Tua Pasta
restaurants.whyGo: Fresh pasta cooked to order at a Borough Market stand, with sauces that change with the season.
restaurants.opNote: Market trading hours only - closed when Borough Market is closed.

restaurants.name: Mercato Metropolitano
restaurants.whyGo: Italian-founded food hall with more than forty traders, heavy on pizza, fresh pasta, arancini and fritto misto.
restaurants.opNote: A venue, not a restaurant - the traders inside change. Six minutes from both Elephant & Castle and Borough.

restaurants.name: PaStation
restaurants.whyGo: Fresh pasta under a tenner in generous portions, near Tottenham Court Road. Built a following online rather than through the guides.

restaurants.name: Artusi
restaurants.whyGo: Peckham dining room doing classically based seasonal cooking with hand-made pasta, at prices well below its central equivalents.

restaurants.name: Bar Italia
restaurants.whyGo: Open since 1949 and still on Frith Street. Coffee, a cannoli and a place to stand at the counter rather than a meal.
restaurants.opNote: Long hours - the traditional Soho late stop. Counter service, minimal seating.

restaurants.name: Mucci's
restaurants.whyGo: Every starter is £10 and every main £20 - one of the first London restaurants to build its whole menu around fixed pricing by course, rather than a time-limited offer.
restaurants.signature: Tuna tartare with avocado and lime gel; 200g sliced sirloin
restaurants.opNote: Owner Giuseppe Mucci introduced the 10/20 pricing so regulars could order without watching the bill. Menu runs from cicchetti through pasta and pizza to steak and fish. Terrace seats around 50. At the World's End end of King's Road, a long walk from any tube - the King's Road buses are the practical way in.

restaurants.name: Locatelli at The National Gallery
restaurants.address: Sainsbury Wing, National Gallery, Trafalgar Square WC2N 5DN
restaurants.whyGo: Giorgio and Plaxy Locatelli's return after Locanda Locatelli closed, on the mezzanine of the Sainsbury Wing. Handmade pasta is the reason to go - the cappellacci stuffed with peas in particular.
restaurants.opNote: 80 seats. Runs on gallery hours, so dinner is early: 11:30-19:30 Sun-Thu, to 22:15 Fri, to 20:15 Sat. Bar Giorgio on the ground floor does espresso and maritozzi for a shorter stop.

restaurants.name: Il Gattopardo
restaurants.whyGo: Massimo Pasquarelli - Abruzzo-born, a decade under Alain Ducasse, previously executive chef at the Ritz-Carlton Singapore - cooking classic Italian on Albemarle Street.
restaurants.opNote: Sharing is encouraged and portions are generous. Three ways to sit: the main room, the light-filled terrace, or the crudo bar. The £20 Pasta & Vino counter offer makes a Mayfair Michelin-listed kitchen unusually reachable.

restaurants.name: Ave Mario
restaurants.whyGo: Big Mamma's Covent Garden room, done as an eighties throwback. Neapolitan pizza, all-homemade pasta and T-bone fiorentina.
restaurants.opNote: Vast and deliberately theatrical - the group books out well ahead and the rooms are loud by design.

restaurants.name: Jacuzzi
restaurants.whyGo: Four storeys on High Street Kensington, and the most seafood-led of the Big Mamma rooms - local fish, Italian caviar, fresh pasta.
restaurants.opNote: The group's grandest London site. Four floors, so ask which one you are seated on.

restaurants.name: Carlotta
restaurants.whyGo: Italian-American rather than Italian - pasta alla vodka and whole roasted fish, in a plush retro dining room on Marylebone High Street.

restaurants.name: Barbarella
restaurants.address: Mackenzie Walk Unit 3 YY, Canary Wharf Estate, London E14 5HX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Big Mamma's Canary Wharf room, done out as a 1970s Cinecittà film studio and named after the Jane Fonda film - T-bone steaks and filled pasta under a lot of glitter.
restaurants.opNote: Opened June 2026. Steps from the Canary Wharf DLR and Jubilee platforms, and a few minutes from the Elizabeth line.

restaurants.name: Crisp Pizza at The Marlborough
restaurants.dietary: Marinara is the only fully vegan pizza
restaurants.whyGo: Carl McCluskey's Crisp, previously only in Hammersmith, brought into central London inside a relaunched Mayfair pub - with the team behind The Devonshire.
restaurants.signature: New Haven pies - traditional, grandma (square, feeds 2-3) and bar pies
restaurants.opNote: TWO VENUES IN ONE. The ground-floor pub is walk-in only and pours Guinness; the pizzeria is in the basement and takes bookings through SevenRooms. IMPORTANT: pizza is not served on Mondays even though the pub is open 11:00-23:00. Pizza runs Tue-Thu 11:30-21:30, Fri-Sat to 22:30, Sun to 20:30.

restaurants.name: Breadstall
restaurants.whyGo: Berwick Street slice counter, on the Soho market street rather than in a dining room.

restaurants.name: Japes
restaurants.whyGo: Dean Street pizza-and-wine room in the middle of Soho.

restaurants.name: Bad Boy Pizza Society
restaurants.address: Seven Dials Market, 35 Earlham St WC2H 9LD
restaurants.whyGo: A pizza counter inside Seven Dials Market, so it comes with the rest of the hall's traders around it.
restaurants.opNote: Trades on Seven Dials Market hours, not its own.

restaurants.name: Sud Italia
restaurants.address: 16 Horner Square, Old Spitalfields Market E1 6EW
restaurants.whyGo: Wood-fired pizza from a stall in Old Spitalfields Market - one of the few genuine market pizzas in central London.
restaurants.opNote: Market trading hours only.

restaurants.name: Dough Hands
restaurants.address: The Spurstowe Arms, 68 Greenwood Rd E8 1AB
restaurants.whyGo: A pizza residency in the back of a Hackney pub - the format that produces some of London's best pizza without a restaurant attached.
restaurants.opNote: Runs on the pub's kitchen hours, which are shorter than the pub's own. Check before travelling.

restaurants.name: Gracey's Pizza
restaurants.address: 1st Floor, Circus Rd S, Battersea Power Station SW11 8DD
restaurants.whyGo: Inside the Battersea Power Station development, on the first floor above the main circus.

restaurants.name: Sarv's Slice
restaurants.whyGo: Slice counter in the Filmworks development by Ealing Broadway.

restaurants.name: Eataly
restaurants.context: Own building - market, restaurants, cafe, cookery school
restaurants.whyGo: Three restaurants, a market of Italian ingredients, a cafe, a takeaway counter and a cookery school, all in one building beside Liverpool Street. Terra has a two-metre wood-fired grill.
restaurants.opNote: A venue rather than a single restaurant - the format varies by which counter or dining room you use. Useful as a wet-weather or with-children option in the City.

restaurants.name: Anima e Cuore
restaurants.address: 127 Kentish Town Rd, London NW1 8PB, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Camden Town room with a reputation well ahead of its prices and its decor.

restaurants.name: Canteen
restaurants.whyGo: A Portobello Road room added to the Michelin Guide in 2026, in its first year.

restaurants.name: Theo Randall at the InterContinental
restaurants.whyGo: Theo Randall spent fifteen years running the kitchen at The River Cafe before opening this Park Lane dining room.
restaurants.opNote: Hotel dining room, so it keeps longer and more reliable hours than most of the independents on this list.

restaurants.name: Sette
restaurants.whyGo: Knightsbridge Italian at the top of the market, and one of very few genuinely ££££ Italians left in London.

restaurants.name: Norma
restaurants.whyGo: Sicilian cooking with the Moorish influence kept in, across four floors of a Fitzrovia townhouse.

restaurants.name: Macellaio RC
restaurants.address: 84 Old Brompton Rd, South Kensington, London SW7 3LQ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A butcher's counter that became a restaurant - Piedmontese Fassona beef hung in the window and cut to order.

restaurants.name: Daphne's
restaurants.whyGo: A Draycott Avenue fixture since 1964, and still the Chelsea room people book for a long lunch.

restaurants.name: Popolo
restaurants.whyGo: A narrow Rivington Street room doing Italian and North African small plates from an open counter.

restaurants.name: Dalla
restaurants.whyGo: One of the Hackney rooms driving the current wave of London Italian cooking away from the centre.

restaurants.name: Elephant Hackney
restaurants.address: 43 Lower Clapton Rd, Lower Clapton, London E5 0NS, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Clapton neighbourhood Italian that Time Out rates among the city's best.

restaurants.name: Lardo
restaurants.address: Unit 3, 201 Richmond Rd, London E8 3NJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A London Fields room with a wood oven, open since 2012 and still on the lists.

restaurants.name: Tiella
restaurants.whyGo: A trattoria run with the sensibility of a pub - strangers talk to each other, and the polpette recipe is a family one.
restaurants.signals: 3 sources: Time Out, The Infatuation, Hot Dinners

restaurants.name: Campania & Jones
restaurants.whyGo: Cooking from the Campania region in a converted dairy near Columbia Road, with pasta made by hand every day.
restaurants.opNote: Close to Columbia Road flower market, so Sunday is a different proposition from the rest of the week.

restaurants.name: Ombra
restaurants.address: 1 Vyner St, Bethnal Green, London E2 9DG, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Named for the Venetian term for a small glass of wine. Fresh pasta, seasonal vegetables and organic wine by the Regent's Canal.

restaurants.name: Sorella
restaurants.whyGo: Robin Gill's Clapham room - the team behind The Dairy - cooking the Amalfi Coast through British produce.

restaurants.name: Noci
restaurants.whyGo: A short, frequently changing pasta menu drawn from across the Italian regions, at prices well below the central equivalents.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Lux Life London, The Sauce Mag

restaurants.name: Osteria Angelina
restaurants.address: 1, Nicholls Clarke Yard, London E1 6SH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Itameshi - Italian cooking through a Japanese lens - with eight fresh pastas made in a glass-walled corner of the dining room.
restaurants.opNote: Sister to Angelina in Dalston, but a different format: Dalston runs a set kaiseki tasting menu, Spitalfields is a la carte and faster. Executive chef Usman Haider oversees both.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Country & Town House, The Infatuation

restaurants.name: Como Garden
restaurants.whyGo: Interiors modelled on the gardens of Lake Como, with handmade pasta and small sharing plates.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Country & Town House, The Sauce Mag

restaurants.name: Chucs Mayfair
restaurants.whyGo: Eight tables of 1950s Riviera glamour on Dover Street, from the clothing brand of the same name.
restaurants.opNote: Very small - eight tables - so booking matters more than the walk-in-friendly rooms elsewhere on this list.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: The Nudge, Lux Life London

restaurants.name: The Dover
restaurants.whyGo: Italian-American cooking on Dover Street, in the mould of a New York supper club.
restaurants.opNote: AMBIGUOUS SOURCE: clustered from a heading that may belong to a neighbouring Dover Street venue. Confirm the identity before publishing.

restaurants.name: Café Murano
restaurants.whyGo: Angela Hartnett's everyday counterpart to Murano - the same kitchen thinking at a third of the price.
restaurants.opNote: Sites in Covent Garden and St James's. The pasta is made fresh at least twice a day.

restaurants.name: St John
restaurants.address: 26 St John St, Barbican, London EC1M 4AY, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Fergus Henderson's whole-animal cooking, open since 1994 and still the argument that longevity is a restaurant's best credential.
restaurants.signature: Roast bone marrow and parsley salad
restaurants.signals: 3 sources: Balance Journal, The Infatuation, Eater London

restaurants.name: The Quality Chop House
restaurants.whyGo: The 1869 room is Grade II listed and the wooden booths are deliberately uncomfortable - it was built as a working man's dining hall and never refitted.

restaurants.name: Quo Vadis
restaurants.whyGo: Karl Marx lived in the building. The dining room below has been feeding Soho since 1926.
restaurants.signals: 3 sources: Balance Journal, The Infatuation, Eater London

restaurants.name: Rochelle Canteen
restaurants.context: Former bike shed of Rochelle School
restaurants.whyGo: Hidden behind a wall in a former school bike shed, with no sign - you ring a buzzer marked 'canteen'.
restaurants.signals: 3 sources: Balance Journal, The Infatuation, Eater London

restaurants.name: The Marksman
restaurants.whyGo: Downstairs is a proper pub; upstairs is the dining room that won Michelin's Pub of the Year.
restaurants.signals: 3 sources: The Infatuation, Eater London, British Food Crew

restaurants.name: The Harwood Arms
restaurants.whyGo: London's only Michelin-starred pub, and the venison comes from the owners' own stalking.
restaurants.signals: 3 sources: Balance Journal, The Infatuation, British Food Crew

restaurants.name: Canton Arms
restaurants.address: 177 S Lambeth Rd, London SW8 1XP, UK
restaurants.whyGo: An old-school South Lambeth boozer that happens to serve one of London's best-regarded roasts.
restaurants.signals: 3 sources: Eater London, Time Out, British Food Crew

restaurants.name: The Devonshire
restaurants.address: The Devonshire, 17 Denman St, London W1D 7HW, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Crowned the UK's number one gastropub in the 2026 Top 50, barely two years after opening. The Guinness pour is the reason half the queue is there.
restaurants.opNote: Charlie Carroll, Ashley Palmer-Watts and Oisin Rogers - the same team behind the Crisp relaunch at The Marlborough. Expect to queue.

restaurants.name: Sweetings
restaurants.address: 39 Queen Victoria St, London EC4N 4SF, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Open since 1889, lunch only, no bookings, and you eat at a counter on a high stool.
restaurants.opNote: Weekday lunch only. No reservations. Closed evenings and weekends entirely.

restaurants.name: The Ledbury
restaurants.whyGo: Brett Graham reopened in 2022 with a tighter focus on British sourcing, and took a third Michelin star.

restaurants.name: The Red Lion & Sun
restaurants.whyGo: 20th in Time Out's 2026 UK gastropub ranking, and the roast Oisin Rogers of The Devonshire sends people to.

restaurants.name: The Camberwell Arms
restaurants.address: 65 Camberwell Church St, London SE5 8TR, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Time Out's top-ranked London gastropub, with roast portions generous enough to be the point.

restaurants.name: The Waterman's Arms
restaurants.whyGo: A Barnes riverside pub, picked out for the setting as much as the roast.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: The Infatuation, British Food Crew

restaurants.name: The Golden Tooth
restaurants.whyGo: A Newington Green pub kitchen that both Time Out and The Infatuation put on their roast lists.

restaurants.name: The Bull
restaurants.whyGo: A Highgate pub with its own brewery attached.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Time Out, British Food Crew

restaurants.name: The Prospect of Whitby
restaurants.whyGo: London's oldest riverside pub, trading since around 1520 - first as The Pelican, then the Devil's Tavern. The 400-year-old stone floor is still there.
restaurants.opNote: Come for the building and the river, not the cooking. The Thames-facing terrace is the reason to time a visit for daylight.
restaurants.signals: Landmark - c.1520, London's oldest riverside pub

restaurants.name: The Spaniards Inn
restaurants.whyGo: Serving since 1585, on the edge of Hampstead Heath by the old toll house. Grade II listed, low beams, and a garden that fills the moment the sun appears.
restaurants.opNote: Pairs naturally with a Heath walk. The toll house makes the lane a single-track pinch point - walk rather than drive.

restaurants.name: The Trafalgar Tavern
restaurants.whyGo: A Regency riverside tavern beside the Old Royal Naval College, historically famous for its whitebait dinners.
restaurants.opNote: Sits directly on the Thames path between the Cutty Sark and the Naval College, so it fits into a Greenwich walk without a detour.
restaurants.signals: Landmark - Regency riverside tavern, Grade II listed

restaurants.name: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese
restaurants.whyGo: Rebuilt in 1667 immediately after the Great Fire, down a Fleet Street alley, across warrens of dark panelled rooms and cellars.
restaurants.opNote: Easy to walk past - the entrance is an unmarked alley off Fleet Street. Multiple floors including cellar bars.
restaurants.signals: Landmark - rebuilt 1667 after the Great Fire

restaurants.name: The George Inn
restaurants.whyGo: The last galleried coaching inn left in London, owned by the National Trust and mentioned by Dickens.
restaurants.opNote: National Trust owned. The courtyard is the point - the surviving gallery runs along one side.
restaurants.signals: Landmark - London's last galleried coaching inn, National Trust

restaurants.name: M Manze
restaurants.whyGo: The oldest surviving pie and mash shop in London, open on Tower Bridge Road since 1902, with the original tiling and marble counters.
restaurants.opNote: Daytime only and closed Sundays, like most pie and mash shops. Liquor is a parsley sauce, not alcohol - worth knowing before ordering.
restaurants.signals: Landmark - London's oldest pie and mash shop, est. 1902

restaurants.name: The Fryer's Delight
restaurants.whyGo: Formica tables, beef dripping, and a room that has not been redecorated in decades. The most-cited chippy in London.
restaurants.signals: 5 sources - the strongest fish-and-chips consensus in London

restaurants.name: Poppies Fish and Chips
restaurants.whyGo: Trading since 1952 and done out as a fifties chip shop, with sites in Spitalfields, Camden, Soho and Notting Hill.

restaurants.name: The Golden Hind
restaurants.whyGo: A Marylebone chippy open since 1914, with the original art deco fryer still standing in the room.

restaurants.name: Fish Central
restaurants.address: 149-155 Central St, King Square, London EC1V 8AP, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Half proper chippy, half sit-down fish restaurant, on the edge of the Old Street roundabout.

restaurants.name: The Seashell of Lisson Grove
restaurants.whyGo: On Lisson Grove since 1964 and frying since before the war - the chippy that draws a celebrity crowd without changing anything about itself.

restaurants.name: Golden Union Fish Bar
restaurants.whyGo: The Soho option, and the one to know if you want fish and chips inside the theatre district.

restaurants.name: Toff's
restaurants.address: 38 Muswell Hill Broadway, Muswell Hill, London N10 3RT, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Muswell Hill's award-winning family chippy, run by the same family since 1988.

restaurants.name: Rock & Sole Plaice
restaurants.whyGo: Claims a lineage back to 1871, with pavement tables on a Covent Garden side street.

restaurants.name: Sutton & Sons
restaurants.dietary: Dedicated vegan menu and a separate vegan site
restaurants.whyGo: Runs a fully vegan chip shop alongside the traditional ones - banana blossom instead of cod.

restaurants.name: Goddards at Greenwich
restaurants.address: 22 King William Walk, London SE10 9HU, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Greenwich pie and mash shop running since 1890, right by the market.

restaurants.name: G. Kelly
restaurants.whyGo: The Roman Road shop, and the east London answer to M Manze's south London one.

restaurants.name: F. Cooke
restaurants.whyGo: One of the last of the old Hackney pie shops, tiled and mirrored and largely unchanged.

restaurants.name: Arment's Pie & Mash
restaurants.address: Pie House, 7-9 Westmoreland Rd, London SE17 2AX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Walworth's pie shop, family-run and still doing eels alongside the pies.

restaurants.name: Maureen's Pie & Mash
restaurants.whyGo: A Chrisp Street pie shop that the guides consistently rate above better-known names.

restaurants.name: Cockney's Pie & Mash
restaurants.whyGo: The west London pie shop, on Portobello Road - the only one of its kind that side of the city.

restaurants.name: BJ's Pie & Mash
restaurants.whyGo: The only pie and mash shop that will swap the mash for chips fried in beef dripping. Cash only.
restaurants.opNote: CASH ONLY - worth knowing before turning up.

restaurants.name: The Eagle
restaurants.whyGo: The pub that invented the gastropub in 1991 - an open kitchen behind the bar and a menu chalked up daily, which every pub in Britain then copied.

restaurants.name: E Pellicci
restaurants.address: 332 Bethnal Grn Rd, London E2 0AG, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Bethnal Green caff run by the same family since 1900, with a Grade II listed marquetry interior and a full English that draws queues.
restaurants.signals: Landmark - est. 1900, Grade II listed interior

restaurants.name: The Parakeet
restaurants.address: 256 Kentish Town Rd, London NW5 2AA, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Kentish Town pub rebuilt around an open fire, and one of the most talked-about openings of recent years.

restaurants.name: The Tamil Prince
restaurants.whyGo: A Victorian pub with a Tamil kitchen behind it - the format London does better than anywhere.

restaurants.name: Blacklock
restaurants.whyGo: Chops cooked over coal and pressed under a Blacklock iron, at prices that undercut every other chophouse in central London.
restaurants.signature: All In - a run of every chop on the menu

restaurants.name: Hawksmoor
restaurants.whyGo: British beef dry-aged and grilled over charcoal, in rooms that were mostly something else first - a brewery, a bank, a ballroom.

restaurants.name: Ken's Fish Bar
restaurants.address: 131 Half Moon Ln, London SE24 9JY, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A south London chippy that three separate guides single out over far better-known names.

restaurants.name: Fish Lounge
restaurants.whyGo: A Clapham chip shop with three guides behind it and none of the tourist traffic of the central ones.

restaurants.name: Robins Pie & Mash
restaurants.whyGo: The north London pie shop, completing the compass alongside M Manze in the south, G. Kelly in the east and Cockney's in the west.

restaurants.name: The Ritz
restaurants.whyGo: The most recognised afternoon tea in London, served in the Palm Court with a pianist and a dress code that is actually enforced.
restaurants.opNote: Jacket and tie required for men; no jeans or trainers. Multiple sittings a day and it books out months ahead.
restaurants.signals: 3 sources: Good Food Guide, Olive Magazine, A Lady in London

restaurants.name: The Wolseley
restaurants.whyGo: A 1920s car showroom turned Viennese-style grand café, and the London power breakfast - as well as the best-value serious afternoon tea.
restaurants.opNote: Does both ends of the day well: breakfast from early, afternoon tea later. The room is the draw either way.
restaurants.signals: 3 sources across breakfast and afternoon-tea passes

restaurants.name: Fortnum & Mason
restaurants.whyGo: The tea merchant's own salon, opened by the Queen in 2012 - the one place where the tea list is the point rather than the cakes.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Olive Magazine, A Lady in London

restaurants.name: The Goring
restaurants.whyGo: The last family-owned grand hotel in London, and the quietest of the big afternoon teas - taken in the garden when the weather allows.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Olive Magazine, A Lady in London

restaurants.name: Sketch
restaurants.whyGo: Afternoon tea inside an art installation - the pink Gallery room and the egg-shaped lavatories are as photographed as the food.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Olive Magazine, A Lady in London

restaurants.name: The Stafford
restaurants.address: 16-18 St James's Pl, London SW1A 1NJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Down a St James's cul-de-sac, with 380-year-old wine cellars beneath and far fewer tourists than the Piccadilly names.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Olive Magazine, A Lady in London

restaurants.name: The Ampersand Hotel
restaurants.address: 10 Harrington Rd, South Kensington, London SW7 3ER, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A themed tea built around the museums on its doorstep - planets, fossils and periodic-table biscuits, which makes it the one that works with children.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Olive Magazine, A Lady in London

restaurants.name: Regency Cafe
restaurants.whyGo: A 1946 black-tiled caff behind Westminster where your name is shouted across the room when the food is up. Cash-friendly, queue out the door, no concessions to anyone.
restaurants.opNote: Closes in the afternoon and all day Sunday. The queue moves fast but forms early at weekends.

restaurants.name: The Pelican
restaurants.address: The Pelican, 45 All Saints Rd, London W11 1HE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Named London's best pub by the Good Food Guide and seventh in the UK - the highest-ranked London entry on that list.
restaurants.signals: Good Food Guide - best London pub, #7 in the UK

restaurants.name: The Bull & Last
restaurants.whyGo: A Highgate Road pub on the edge of Hampstead Heath, 39th in the UK gastropub rankings.
restaurants.opNote: NOT the same pub as The Bull, which is also in Highgate and also on this list. Different sites, different owners - keep the two rows distinct.

restaurants.name: The Knave of Clubs
restaurants.address: 25 Bethnal Grn Rd, London E1 6HT, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Bethnal Green Road pub that reached 43rd in the UK gastropub rankings soon after opening.

restaurants.name: Unity Diner
restaurants.whyGo: Traditional British cooking done entirely without animal products - the place the vegan community names when asked for British food rather than international.
restaurants.opNote: Non-profit; surplus goes to animal welfare work. The only fully vegan British kitchen on this list.

restaurants.name: Burro
restaurants.address: Unit 2, Floral Court, Floral St, London WC2E 9FB, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Named by both The Infatuation and Time Out, and one of the few Italian openings to reach two independent guides quickly.

restaurants.name: Casa Felicia
restaurants.whyGo: A Queen's Park neighbourhood Italian picked up by Time Out and named a finalist in The Italian Awards.
restaurants.signals: 2 sources: Time Out, The Italian Awards 2026

restaurants.name: Trishna
restaurants.whyGo: Michelin-starred cooking from India's south-west coast, and the most-cited Indian restaurant in London across every guide we read.
restaurants.signals: 6 sources - the strongest Indian consensus; Michelin star

restaurants.name: BiBi
restaurants.address: 42 N Audley St, London W1K 6ZP, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Chet Sharma's Mayfair room, cooking regional Indian dishes through a fine-dining lens with a drinks list built to match.

restaurants.name: Brigadiers
restaurants.whyGo: Built on the Indian army mess-bar idea - big rooms, sport on the screens, whisky, and barbecue over coals. The loudest Indian restaurant in the City, by design.

restaurants.name: Dishoom
restaurants.whyGo: The Irani cafes of old Bombay recreated in careful detail, and the bacon naan roll that made it a breakfast destination as much as a dinner one.
restaurants.opNote: Any party size can book before 6pm; after 6pm bookings are for groups of six or more only. Most tables are held back for walk-ins either way. Seven London branches; the Branches tab has six named.
restaurants.signals: 4 sources; also a 3-source pick on the breakfast pass

restaurants.name: Gymkhana
restaurants.whyGo: Modelled on the colonial-era gymkhana clubs of India, and the highest-decorated Indian kitchen in the city.

restaurants.name: Jamavar
restaurants.whyGo: Named for the handwoven Kashmiri shawl, cooking across the whole subcontinent rather than one region of it.

restaurants.name: Veeraswamy
restaurants.address: Victory House, 99 Regent St., London W1B 4RS, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Open since 1926 and the oldest surviving Indian restaurant in Britain, above Regent Street, with a Michelin star to go with the history.

restaurants.name: Benares
restaurants.whyGo: Named Best Fine Dining Restaurant in London at the Asian Curry Awards, and a Berkeley Square fixture for two decades.
restaurants.signals: Asian Curry Awards - Best Fine Dining, London

restaurants.name: Darjeeling Express
restaurants.whyGo: Asma Khan's kitchen, staffed entirely by women, cooking the food of Calcutta and the royal Mughlai tradition she grew up in.

restaurants.name: The Cinnamon Club
restaurants.address: The Old Westminster Library, Great Smith St, London SW1P 3BU, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Inside the Grade II listed old Westminster Library, bookshelves still in place - the most unusual dining room of any Indian restaurant in London.

restaurants.name: Shree Krishna Vada Pav
restaurants.whyGo: Vada pav - the Mumbai potato-fritter roll - done properly and cheaply, from a counter rather than a dining room.

restaurants.name: Kutir
restaurants.whyGo: A Chelsea townhouse done as an Indian hunting lodge, with a menu built around game and the outdoors.

restaurants.name: Kokum
restaurants.address: 58-60 E Dulwich Rd, London SE22 9AX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Named for the sour coastal fruit, cooking the seafood traditions of India's western shore.

restaurants.name: Kricket
restaurants.whyGo: Started in a Brixton shipping container and grew into several sites, doing Indian cooking as small plates rather than curries.

restaurants.name: Amaya
restaurants.address: Off Lowndes St, London SW1X 8JT, UK
restaurants.whyGo: An open kitchen of tawa, sigri and tandoor in Belgravia, with a Michelin star for grilling rather than saucing.

restaurants.name: Kanishka
restaurants.whyGo: Atul Kochhar cooking the north-eastern states - Assam, Nagaland, Sikkim - which almost nowhere else in London attempts.

restaurants.name: Empire Empire
restaurants.whyGo: A love letter to 1970s Bombay dining rooms, from the JKS group - velvet, brass and disco-era styling.

restaurants.name: Colonel Saab
restaurants.whyGo: Inside the old Holborn Town Hall, filled with the owner's family collection of Indian antiques. Named Asian Restaurant of the Year for London.
restaurants.signals: Asian Curry Awards - Asian Restaurant of the Year, London

restaurants.name: Babur
restaurants.whyGo: A Brockley dining room that has been quietly outcooking most of central London for over thirty years.

restaurants.name: Namaaste Highgate
restaurants.whyGo: Named Asian Restaurant of the Year for London at the 2025 Asian Curry Awards - a neighbourhood restaurant that beat the Mayfair field.
restaurants.signals: Asian Curry Awards - Asian Restaurant of the Year, London

restaurants.name: Punjab
restaurants.whyGo: Open since 1946 and claimed as the oldest North Indian restaurant in Britain, still run by the same family.

restaurants.name: City Spice
restaurants.whyGo: The Brick Lane curry house that gets named most often when people argue about which of them is still worth eating at.

restaurants.name: Sheba
restaurants.whyGo: A long-standing Brick Lane room, picked out on a TOPJAW run through the street.

restaurants.name: Quilon
restaurants.whyGo: Michelin-starred cooking from Kerala and the Malabar coast - the one starred kitchen in London doing south-western seafood rather than northern grills.

restaurants.name: Tamarind
restaurants.whyGo: The first Indian restaurant in the world to win a Michelin star, and still a Mayfair basement doing tandoor cooking at that level.

restaurants.name: The Bombay Restaurant
restaurants.address: Opposite Gloucester Road Tube, Courtfield Rd, South Kensington, London SW7 4QH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Named by three independent sources including Currylife, which covers the curry-house trade rather than the restaurant press.
restaurants.signals: 3 sources - the strongest of the remaining tier

restaurants.name: Madhu's
restaurants.whyGo: Punjabi cooking by way of Kenya - the East African Asian tradition that Southall does better than anywhere else in Britain.

restaurants.name: Masala Zone
restaurants.whyGo: Thalis and street-food plates at prices well below the Mayfair rooms, from the group behind Amaya and Chutney Mary.

restaurants.name: Pahli Hill Bandra Bhai
restaurants.whyGo: Named for the Bandra hill district of Bombay, with a basement bar that runs later than the dining room above it.

restaurants.name: The Tamil Crown
restaurants.whyGo: The second pub from the Tamil Prince team, doing the same Tamil-kitchen-in-a-Victorian-boozer format that London does better than anywhere.
restaurants.opNote: Sibling to The Tamil Prince, also in Islington - two separate pubs, not two names for one.

restaurants.name: Tamila
restaurants.whyGo: Tamil home cooking in Clapham, picked up by both the Good Food Guide and Time Out.

restaurants.name: Udaya Kerala Restaurant
restaurants.whyGo: Keralan cooking - appam, coastal fish, coconut - rather than the northern menu most London curry houses run.

restaurants.name: Hyderabadi Spice
restaurants.address: 309 High St N, London E12 6SL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Hyderabadi biryani done as its own tradition rather than as a side dish on a north Indian menu.

restaurants.name: Vatavaran
restaurants.whyGo: Cooking from the Himalayan foothills - a region almost nowhere else in London represents.

restaurants.name: Shankeys
restaurants.whyGo: Named by both The Infatuation and Time Out, which is a narrow overlap to land in.

restaurants.name: Rasa
restaurants.whyGo: An all-vegetarian Keralan kitchen behind a shocking pink shopfront, cooking with coconut and curry leaf rather than cream.

restaurants.name: Saravanaa Bhavan
restaurants.whyGo: The London outpost of the Chennai vegetarian chain, and the cheapest way in the West End to eat a properly made masala dosa.

restaurants.name: Horn OK Please
restaurants.whyGo: Samosa chaat built to order - the samosas crushed under chickpea curry, yoghurt and tamarind while still hot - from an all-vegetarian Borough Market stall.

restaurants.name: Gujarati Rasoi
restaurants.whyGo: Mother-and-son Gujarati cooking from family recipes - thalis, bhajia and dhal - at a market where almost everything else is European.

restaurants.name: Kolkati
restaurants.whyGo: Kati rolls the Kolkata way - paratha cooked with egg through it, wrapped round spiced chicken or paneer with pickled onion and lime.

restaurants.name: Fallow
restaurants.whyGo: Whole-animal and root-to-stem cooking pushed further than anywhere else in London - offcuts, byproducts and discarded species treated as the menu rather than a footnote.
restaurants.opNote: Runs a Sunday roast and a breakfast service as well, which is why it surfaced on both of those passes rather than on a best-British listicle.

restaurants.name: Brat
restaurants.whyGo: Tomos Parry cooking over open fire above a Shoreditch pub, built around whole turbot in a custom grill.

restaurants.name: Core by Clare Smyth
restaurants.address: 92 Kensington Park Rd, London W11 2PN, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Three Michelin stars, built on British produce rather than French technique - widely called the most technically accomplished table in the city.

restaurants.name: Noble Rot
restaurants.whyGo: Started as a wine magazine and became a restaurant - the list is the point and the kitchen is built to serve it.

restaurants.name: Café Deco
restaurants.whyGo: A short daily-changing menu on Store Street, out of the Rochelle Canteen and Quality Chop House lineage.

restaurants.name: 40 Maltby Street
restaurants.whyGo: A natural-wine importer's arch serving food off a blackboard - the original of the Bermondsey arch format everyone else copied.
restaurants.opNote: Small, largely no-bookings, and closed more days than it opens. Check before travelling.

restaurants.name: Cafe Cecilia
restaurants.whyGo: Max Rocha's canalside room in Hackney - short menu, St John lineage, and a guinness cake with its own following.

restaurants.name: Simpson's in the Strand
restaurants.whyGo: Roasts carved from silver trolleys at the table, in a dining room that has been doing exactly that since the 1820s.

restaurants.name: Hide
restaurants.whyGo: Three floors above Green Park with the Hedonism wine cellar underneath - the list runs to thousands of bins.

restaurants.name: Sunday
restaurants.whyGo: A tiny Barnsbury room that built its name on brunch queues rather than dinner service.
restaurants.opNote: No bookings at weekends. The queue is the experience and it starts early.

restaurants.name: The Langham
restaurants.whyGo: The Palm Court claims to be where the afternoon tea ritual began in the 1860s, and it is still the benchmark other hotel salons are measured against.
restaurants.signals: 4 domains - joint highest of the afternoon-tea pass

restaurants.name: The Dorchester
restaurants.whyGo: Served the length of the Promenade, opening with a glass of Veuve Clicquot poured tableside. The grand end of Mayfair, where Brown's is the club-like one.

restaurants.name: The Lanesborough
restaurants.address: Hyde, Park Corner, London SW1X 7TA, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Taken under the glass dome of the Céleste dining room at Hyde Park Corner - the brightest of the grand-hotel rooms rather than the most gilded.

restaurants.name: Claridge's
restaurants.whyGo: Art Deco Mayfair with its own house blend of Assam and Darjeeling, served in the Foyer and Reading Room. The default answer when someone asks for the traditional one.

restaurants.name: The Savoy
restaurants.whyGo: Under the glass cupola of the Thames Foyer, with a pianist, in London's first purpose-built luxury hotel.

restaurants.name: Brown's Hotel
restaurants.whyGo: The intimate, club-like Mayfair option - panelled and low-ceilinged where The Dorchester is a long bright promenade.

restaurants.name: The Berkeley
restaurants.address: The Berkeley, Wilton Pl, London SW1X 7RL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Pastries modelled on the current season's runway - handbags, heels, a new collection each time the shows change. The one that is about fashion rather than heritage.

restaurants.name: The Connaught
restaurants.address: The Connaught, Carlos Pl, London W1K 2AL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Understated where the rest of Mayfair is gilded - precision and craft rather than spectacle, and cheaper Monday to Thursday.

restaurants.name: Mandarin Oriental Hyde Park
restaurants.whyGo: The Rosebery lounge backs onto Hyde Park, which makes it the one grand tea with a garden view rather than a street.

restaurants.name: Rosewood London
restaurants.whyGo: Taken in the Mirror Room of a Belle Epoque building off High Holborn - the grand-hotel format outside the Mayfair cluster.

restaurants.name: One Aldwych
restaurants.style: Charlie and the Chocolate Factory tea
restaurants.whyGo: A themed tea built around Charlie and the Chocolate Factory - the one that works with children who would be bored by a Mayfair salon.

restaurants.name: The Milestone Hotel
restaurants.whyGo: A small townhouse hotel opposite Kensington Palace - the quietest of the listed teas, and the only one in Kensington.

restaurants.name: Four Seasons
restaurants.whyGo: Roast duck hanging in the window and a queue outside for it - the most-cited Chinese restaurant in London across every guide read.

restaurants.name: Plum Valley
restaurants.whyGo: A family-run Gerrard Street room in a black-fronted building, doing award-winning dim sum in a smarter setting than most of Chinatown.

restaurants.name: Tao Tao Ju
restaurants.whyGo: Towering bamboo baskets of steamed and grilled dim sum, made fresh on site each day - the refined end of Lisle Street.

restaurants.name: Bun House
restaurants.whyGo: Steamed buns from a counter rather than a dining room, at a price that undercuts everything around it.

restaurants.name: Wong Kei
restaurants.whyGo: A Wardour Street institution over several floors, famous for decades for brusque service and prices nothing central can match.
restaurants.opNote: Cash was the rule for years and the service style is part of the legend. Fast, loud, and not a place to linger.

restaurants.name: Chinatown Bakery
restaurants.whyGo: Egg tarts and bolo bao made in the window on Newport Place - the queue is usually visible from the gate.

restaurants.name: Dim Sum & Duck
restaurants.address: 124 King's Cross Rd, London WC1X 9DS, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Dim sum served day and night rather than only until mid-afternoon, which almost nowhere else in London does.

restaurants.name: Hunan
restaurants.whyGo: No menu at all - you say what you dislike and dishes keep arriving until you stop them. Hunanese cooking, changing daily.
restaurants.opNote: There is no a la carte. The kitchen decides, which is the whole proposition - say in advance if you have restrictions.

restaurants.name: Etles Uyghur Restaurant
restaurants.whyGo: Uyghur cooking from Xinjiang - hand-pulled laghman, cumin lamb skewers, a tradition almost nowhere else in London represents.

restaurants.name: Dream Xi'An
restaurants.whyGo: Xi'an cooking - biang biang noodles, roujiamo, the food of the Silk Road's eastern end.

restaurants.name: Canton Blue
restaurants.address: The Peninsula, 1 Grosvenor Pl, London SW1X 7HJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Inside The Peninsula, themed on a 19th-century trading ship - the most expensive Cantonese room in London and built to look it.

restaurants.name: Dim Sum Library
restaurants.whyGo: Dim sum in a bar-led room rather than a banquet hall, which makes it the one that works for an evening rather than a lunch.

restaurants.name: Dumplings' Legend
restaurants.whyGo: A glass-walled kitchen on Gerrard Street where the xiao long bao are folded in front of the queue.

restaurants.name: Cafe TPT
restaurants.whyGo: A Wardour Street cha chaan teng - Hong Kong cafe food, late hours, and none of the tourist pricing of the main drag.

restaurants.name: Golden Phoenix
restaurants.whyGo: A Chinatown Cantonese room that both Time Out and The Hotel Journal single out from a very crowded street.

restaurants.name: Chinese Tapas House
restaurants.address: 15 Little Newport St, London WC2H 7JJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Northern Chinese cooking served as small plates, which is a rarer format here than the Cantonese banquet.

restaurants.name: Kung Fu Noodle
restaurants.whyGo: Noodles pulled to order in the window - the cheapest proper cooked meal in Chinatown.

restaurants.name: A. Wong
restaurants.address: 70 Wilton Rd, Pimlico, London SW1V 1DE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The only two-Michelin-starred Chinese restaurant in Europe, working through the regional cooking of the whole country across a tasting menu.
restaurants.opNote: Dim sum at lunch is a different and far cheaper proposition than the evening tasting menu - the two services barely resemble each other.

restaurants.name: Hakkasan
restaurants.whyGo: The basement room on Hanway Place that made high-end Chinese food fashionable in London, and set the template every glossy Chinese dining room since has borrowed from.
restaurants.signals: Michelin star 2020-2023, lost in the 2024 guide

restaurants.name: Yauatcha
restaurants.whyGo: All-day dim sum with a patisserie counter downstairs, from the Hakkasan founder - it held a star for fourteen years and still cooks like it.

restaurants.name: Park Chinois
restaurants.whyGo: A 1930s Shanghai supper club recreated on Berkeley Street, with live music downstairs and cabaret rather than a quiet dinner.

restaurants.name: Imperial Treasure
restaurants.whyGo: The London arm of the Singapore group, doing Cantonese cooking at a level and price that assumes you know what you are ordering.

restaurants.name: Min Jiang
restaurants.address: 2, 24 Kensington High St, London W8 4PT, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Wood-fired Peking duck carved tableside on the tenth floor, looking over Kensington Gardens - the only Chinese room in London with that view.

restaurants.name: Royal China
restaurants.whyGo: A black-and-gold banquet hall on Baker Street where weekend dim sum runs at the volume of an airport terminal, and the queue is part of it.
restaurants.opNote: No bookings at weekend lunch - the busiest dim sum service in London and it moves fast.

restaurants.name: Baba Tang
restaurants.address: 109 King's Cross Rd, London WC1X 9LR, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Topped Time Out's dim sum ranking, with everything made in house - the cheung fun with peanut and XO sauce is the dish people go for.
restaurants.signature: Cheung fun with peanut and XO
restaurants.signals: Time Out - best dim sum in London

restaurants.name: Joy King Lau
restaurants.whyGo: Four floors off Leicester Square doing trolley-era dim sum the old way, largely unchanged while the street around it turned over.

restaurants.name: The Duck and Rice
restaurants.whyGo: Alan Yau put a Chinese kitchen inside a Berwick Street pub - copper tanks downstairs, dining room above. The format has no real equivalent.

restaurants.name: Sichuan Folk
restaurants.whyGo: Proper Sichuan heat off Brick Lane, in a stretch better known for curry houses.

restaurants.name: Kai Mayfair
restaurants.address: 65 S Audley St, London W1K 2QU, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Held a Michelin star for the best part of two decades on South Audley Street, cooking Chinese food for Mayfair rather than adapting Mayfair to it.

restaurants.name: Pearl Liang
restaurants.whyGo: An unexpectedly large basement dining room behind Paddington station, routinely rated above the Chinatown equivalents by people who eat a lot of Cantonese food.
restaurants.opNote: Five set menus, built for a table that wants to share rather than order individually.

restaurants.name: Xi'an Impression
restaurants.whyGo: A small room opposite the Emirates doing the chewy, chilli-oil-heavy cooking of Shaanxi - the liangpi cold noodles are the reason people cross London for it.
restaurants.opNote: No bookings, and the room is tiny - go off-peak or expect to wait.

restaurants.name: Murger Han
restaurants.whyGo: Named after the murger - slow-cooked meat packed into a flatbread bun - and one of the cheapest serious lunches in the City if you know to order it.

restaurants.name: Yi-Ban
restaurants.address: Regatta Centre, 1010 Dockside Rd, London E16 2QT, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Dim sum over the water at the Royal Docks, trading since 2003 and almost entirely unknown to central London.

restaurants.name: The Eight
restaurants.whyGo: A cha chaan teng - the Hong Kong cafe format, where condensed-milk toast and macaroni soup sit on the same menu as rice plates.

restaurants.name: Orient London
restaurants.whyGo: The smart end of Chinatown - several floors on Wardour Street where the room is doing as much work as the trolley.

restaurants.name: Kung Fu Burger
restaurants.whyGo: Everything is built on a sourdough Chinese-style bun, drawing on street food from across East and South East Asia rather than one region.

restaurants.name: Shan Shui Social
restaurants.whyGo: Cantonese and Sichuan cooking in a room styled on 1920s Shanghai, a minute from Victoria station - from Ellen Chew's Chew on This group.

restaurants.name: BaoziInn
restaurants.whyGo: Northern Chinese street food tidied up for London, in a room done out in Communist-era poster kitsch.

restaurants.name: Jixiang Baozi
restaurants.whyGo: A counter turning out baozi from bamboo steamers, sold to eat standing up rather than sat down.

restaurants.name: Borough Market
restaurants.whyGo: Traders have sold food on this site since the thirteenth century, and the mix still leans hard on British and European produce - cheese, charcuterie, bread, oysters - alongside cooked stalls from a dozen countries.
restaurants.opNote: Busiest between 11am and 2pm on Saturdays. Friday mid-morning is the quietest window with everything still stocked.

restaurants.name: Kappacasein
restaurants.whyGo: Bill Oglethorpe scrapes melted raclette straight off the wheel onto new potatoes, with cornichons and pickled onions. The queue is the landmark.
restaurants.opNote: Market trading hours only. The queue is longest at Saturday lunch.

restaurants.name: Hobbs Roast
restaurants.whyGo: Roast pork with stuffing and apple sauce in a baguette, plus turkey and salt beef versions - a Sunday lunch reduced to something you can eat walking.
restaurants.signature: Roast loin of pork with stuffing and apple sauce

restaurants.name: Richard Haward's Oysters
restaurants.whyGo: Mersea oysters shucked in front of you by a family that has been farming them since the 1700s, with a few pavement tables and a glass of wine.

restaurants.name: Bread Ahead
restaurants.address: Borough Market, Cathedral St, London SE1 9DE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The creme brulee doughnut is blowtorched in front of you. It started as one Borough stall and is now a bakery school and a small chain.

restaurants.name: Maltby Street Market
restaurants.address: Arch 46, Ropewalk, Maltby St, London SE1 3PA, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A run of railway arches off Bermondsey that started in 2009 as the scrappy alternative to Borough, and is now the main contender to it.
restaurants.opNote: Weekends only - it is not a weekday destination.

restaurants.name: Seven Dials Market
restaurants.whyGo: A former banana warehouse off Seven Dials, curated rather than sprawling - the most useful food hall in the centre if you are with people who all want something different.

restaurants.name: Pick & Cheese
restaurants.address: Seven Dials Market, Short's Gardens, London WC2H 9AT, UK
restaurants.whyGo: British cheeses ride past on a conveyor belt, each paired with its own condiment - a gimmick that turns out to be the best way to taste a lot of them in one sitting.

restaurants.name: Arcade Food Hall
restaurants.address: 103-105 New Oxford St, London WC1A 1DB, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Less a food court than a set of proper kitchens under one roof - residents have included Plaza Khao Gaeng and Supa Ya Ramen rather than generic concessions.

restaurants.name: Old Spitalfields Market
restaurants.whyGo: A Victorian covered market on the City fringe where the food traders sit alongside the stalls, so lunch and browsing are the same trip.

restaurants.name: Broadway Market
restaurants.whyGo: A Saturday street market running down towards the canal, weighted towards British producers, and the reason half of Hackney is outdoors on a Saturday morning.
restaurants.opNote: Saturday is the main market. Much quieter and largely shut the rest of the week.

restaurants.name: Market Halls Victoria
restaurants.whyGo: A converted ticket hall beside Victoria station - the most useful eating option in an area that is otherwise chains and commuters.

restaurants.name: Camden Market
restaurants.address: 54-56 Camden Lock Pl, London NW1 8AF, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The largest concentration of cooked street food in London, canalside at Camden Lock - very little of it British, and that is rather the point.
restaurants.opNote: Busiest at weekends. Weekday lunch is the same food without the crush.

restaurants.name: 45 Jermyn St
restaurants.whyGo: Beef Wellington and lobster spaghetti finished at the table, coupes and floats for pudding - a brasserie doing the theatrical old-school service almost nobody still does.
restaurants.signature: Beef Wellington, carved at the table
restaurants.opNote: Open 8am to 10pm through the week, so it covers breakfast and late dinner as well as lunch.

restaurants.name: Mount St. Restaurant
restaurants.address: First Floor, 41-43 Mount St, London W1K 2RX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Over 200 works of art hang in the room - Warhol, Freud, Picasso - above a Mayfair pub, with a menu drawn from the cooking history of London itself.

restaurants.name: The Mayfair Chippy
restaurants.whyGo: Fish and chips treated as a restaurant dish rather than a takeaway, with oysters, crab and mussels alongside - trading since 2015 and carrying an AA rosette for it.
restaurants.signature: The Mayfair Classic fish and chips
restaurants.opNote: Seven days a week for lunch and dinner. Takeaway runs alongside the dining room.

restaurants.name: Shoreditch Fish and Chips
restaurants.whyGo: A 1960s-styled chip shop near Brick Lane doing the traditional version straight, with sauces thrown in rather than charged for.

restaurants.name: Corinthia London
restaurants.address: Corinthia Hotel, 10 Whitehall Pl, London SW1A 2BD, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Tea under a Baccarat crystal chandelier with a Steinway playing, and a tea master who weighs and blends each infusion to order.

restaurants.name: The Cadogan
restaurants.whyGo: A Belmond drawing room on Sloane Street with a pianist playing through the service - the quiet end of the London tea circuit rather than the spectacle end.

restaurants.name: Jumeirah Carlton Tower
restaurants.whyGo: The Chinoiserie tea room serves daily rather than in sittings, which makes it one of the easier Knightsbridge teas to get into at short notice.

restaurants.name: The Laundry
restaurants.whyGo: A former Edwardian laundry off Coldharbour Lane, running from breakfast through to dinner with a wine shop attached - the kitchen genuinely does not stop.
restaurants.opNote: Food served all day and into the evening, so it works at the awkward hours most neighbourhood restaurants do not cover.

restaurants.name: Petersham Nurseries
restaurants.address: Church Ln, Petersham Rd, Richmond TW10 7AB, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Lunch inside a working plant nursery, under glass and surrounded by what is for sale - the setting is the entire proposition and nothing in London repeats it.
restaurants.opNote: Lunch-led. The Richmond site and the Covent Garden one are different propositions - check which you are booking.

restaurants.name: Mae + Harvey
restaurants.whyGo: A corner cafe on Roman Road with a menu that changes weekly - Turkish eggs, house-cured salmon, roast plum pancakes - rather than a fixed brunch list repeated all year.

restaurants.name: Sushi Tetsu
restaurants.whyGo: Seven seats at a pale hinoki counter in a Clerkenwell alley, run by Toru Takahashi and his wife Harumi - and only them, which is why it is the hardest table in London to get.
restaurants.opNote: Seven seats and a two-person operation. Booking opens in windows and goes almost immediately.

restaurants.name: The Araki
restaurants.whyGo: A no-choice menu at around £310, built on rare ingredients and served in two sittings a night to a handful of people.
restaurants.opNote: Tuesday to Saturday only, two sittings. Closed Sunday and Monday.

restaurants.name: Sushi Kanesaka
restaurants.whyGo: Thirteen covers inside 45 Park Lane - nine at the counter, four in a private room - doing omakase only, from the Tokyo original.
restaurants.opNote: Omakase only, no a la carte. Opened July 2023.

restaurants.name: Dinings SW3
restaurants.address: Walton House, Lennox Gardens Mews, Walton St, London SW3 2JH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The most-cited Japanese room in London across these sources - izakaya-scale plates done at sushi-counter precision, with a courtyard that most guides forget to mention.
restaurants.signals: 5 consensus domains - the highest of any Japanese venue here

restaurants.name: Sushi Atelier
restaurants.address: 114 Great Portland St, London W1W 6PH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Repeatedly named the best-value serious omakase in central London - the same counter discipline as the Mayfair rooms at a fraction of the outlay.

restaurants.name: Kurisu Omakase
restaurants.whyGo: Eighteen courses in Brixton, where chef Chris Restrepo runs Japanese technique through his Thai-Colombian background - the least likely omakase address in London and one of the best.

restaurants.name: Umu
restaurants.whyGo: Kaiseki in the Kyoto tradition - a fixed seasonal progression rather than a sushi counter, which makes it the odd one out among Mayfair's Japanese rooms.

restaurants.name: Zuma
restaurants.whyGo: Opened in 2002 and effectively invented the London template for informal, izakaya-inspired Japanese dining - since exported to 27 sites across four continents.

restaurants.name: Roka
restaurants.whyGo: The robata grill sits in the middle of the room and everything comes off it - open since 2003 and still the reference point for the format in London.
restaurants.signature: Black cod on a hoba leaf

restaurants.name: Nobu Old Park Lane
restaurants.address: 19 Old Park Ln, London W1K 1LB, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The original London Nobu, and the room that put miso black cod on menus worldwide.

restaurants.name: The Aubrey
restaurants.whyGo: A maximalist take on a Ginza night out inside the Mandarin Oriental - closer to a bar with exceptional food than a hotel dining room.

restaurants.name: Jin Kichi
restaurants.whyGo: A small family-run izakaya on Heath Street doing charcoal yakitori at prices that have never caught up with the postcode.

restaurants.name: Himi
restaurants.whyGo: The first solo restaurant from the team behind Roji, opened in January 2025 on Newburgh Street.

restaurants.name: Kanada-Ya
restaurants.address: 64 St Giles High St, London WC2H 8LE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The broth recipe was worked out in Fukuoka before the first London site opened, and the queue outside the St Giles branch has become part of the experience.
restaurants.opNote: No bookings. The queue is shortest before noon and after 2pm.

restaurants.name: Monohon Ramen
restaurants.whyGo: A single-site ramen bar on Old Street that takes no reservations and has outlasted most of the chains that opened around it.
restaurants.opNote: No reservations - walk in and wait.

restaurants.name: Bone Daddies
restaurants.address: 14A Old Compton St, London W1D 4TJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Ramen with a deliberate Western slant and a soundtrack to match - the bowl that made ramen a night out in London rather than a quick lunch.

restaurants.name: Shoryu Ramen
restaurants.whyGo: Hakata-style tonkotsu across a spread of central sites, which makes it the ramen you can actually get into when the single-site places have queues out the door.

restaurants.name: Koya
restaurants.whyGo: Udon made by hand at their own noodle workshop, served from breakfast onwards - the Frith Street counter has been doing it since 2010.
restaurants.opNote: Opens for a Japanese breakfast service that almost nothing else in Soho offers.

restaurants.name: Koya Ko
restaurants.whyGo: The Broadway Market outpost, opened in 2021 - the same handmade udon without the Soho queue.

restaurants.name: Marugame Udon
restaurants.whyGo: A canteen where you walk the line past the open kitchen watching the noodles rolled, cut and boiled - the cheapest proper udon in London and the most fun to queue for.

restaurants.name: Tanakatsu
restaurants.whyGo: A kitchen built around the cutlet - generous katsu sets near Angel station at prices that make it a regular rather than an occasion.

restaurants.name: Eat Tokyo
restaurants.address: 14 N End Rd, London NW11 7PH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Enormous portions, Japanese chefs and prices that have barely moved - the volume option that Japanese Londoners actually use.

restaurants.name: Angelina
restaurants.whyGo: A fixed menu that runs Japanese technique through Italian dishes without treating either as a novelty - the only kitchen in London doing it seriously.

restaurants.name: Akira at Japan House
restaurants.whyGo: Inside Japan House, sourcing directly from Japan where it can - the bento and donburi use produce that otherwise never reaches a London menu.

restaurants.name: Tokyo Sukiyaki-Tei
restaurants.whyGo: A wagyu specialist doing sukiyaki and shabu-shabu - hotpot cooked at the table, which almost nowhere else in London offers properly.

restaurants.name: AUN
restaurants.address: 178 Stoke Newington Church St, London N16 0JL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A small independent in Stoke Newington working to wakon yosai - Japanese spirit, Western technique - as a tasting menu rather than a sushi counter.

restaurants.name: Chisou
restaurants.whyGo: Open since 2002 and seconds from Oxford Circus - the most central serious Japanese room in London, which is most of the point of it.

restaurants.name: Cocoro
restaurants.whyGo: Open since 2006 and the sort of place Japanese office groups and families actually eat - sushi, sukiyaki and a tonkotsu ramen that punches above the room.

restaurants.name: Engawa
restaurants.whyGo: Built around certified Kobe beef, which very few London kitchens are licensed to serve - the sushi is good but the beef is the reason to book.

restaurants.name: Hakata Ramen + Bar
restaurants.whyGo: Named for the Fukuoka district the style comes from, doing Kyushu tonkotsu on Bermondsey Street with enough room to actually sit down.

restaurants.name: Los Mochis Notting Hill
restaurants.whyGo: Sashimi and maki on the same menu as ceviche, tiradito and tacos - the pairing sounds like a gimmick and is served like neither cuisine is being humoured.

restaurants.name: Nobu Portman Square
restaurants.whyGo: The newer of the two London Nobus and the calmer one - a hotel dining room rather than the Old Park Lane scene.

restaurants.name: Ramo Ramen
restaurants.address: 157 Kentish Town Rd, London NW1 8PD, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Ramen run through Filipino cooking rather than beside it - the oxtail kare kare bowl is the dish the whole place is built around.

restaurants.name: TOKii
restaurants.address: 50 Great Cumberland Pl, Marble Arch, London W1H 7FD, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The dining room of a Japanese-run Marylebone hotel, which shows in the detail - and it serves a proper Japanese breakfast, which almost no London hotel does.

restaurants.name: Tonkotsu
restaurants.whyGo: Launched in Soho in 2012 by Ken Yamada and Emma Reynolds, making its own noodles - and now the ramen you are never more than a short walk from.
restaurants.opNote: Around 18 sites across the UK. Reliable rather than remarkable, which is the useful thing about it.

restaurants.name: Al Waha
restaurants.whyGo: The most-cited Lebanese room in London across these sources - white walls, hanging foliage and mezze taken seriously rather than served as filler.
restaurants.signals: 4 consensus domains - the joint highest here

restaurants.name: Bubala
restaurants.whyGo: Entirely vegetarian and almost never described that way - the point is that nobody at the table notices what is missing.

restaurants.name: Imad's Syrian Kitchen
restaurants.address: 2.5, Top Floor, Kingly Ct, Carnaby St, Carnaby, London W1B 5PW, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Imad Alarnab cooked his way from Damascus to a Kingly Court balcony - the Syrian home cooking is the draw and the story is not decoration.

restaurants.name: Ishbilia
restaurants.whyGo: A Knightsbridge Lebanese that has held its regulars for decades - the mezze list runs long enough that ordering is the hard part.

restaurants.name: Mr Falafel
restaurants.address: Units T4/T5, New Shepherds Bush Market, Uxbridge Rd, London W12 8LH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Palestinian falafel from a market stall in Shepherd's Bush, and the one name that appears on every falafel list in London.

restaurants.name: Akub
restaurants.whyGo: Fadi Kattan opened Fawda in Bethlehem before bringing Palestinian cooking to a Notting Hill townhouse - the first London kitchen to treat it as a fine-dining cuisine.
restaurants.signals: Time Out Top 50 Restaurants in London

restaurants.name: The Palomar
restaurants.whyGo: The zinc counter, not the tables - sit at it and the cooking happens a foot from your plate, with the room loud enough to make it a night out.

restaurants.name: Honey & Co
restaurants.address: 54 Lamb's Conduit St, London WC1N 3LW, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Sarit Packer and Itamar Srulovich cook the food they write about, in rooms small enough that the kitchen is effectively at your table.

restaurants.name: Ottolenghi
restaurants.whyGo: The window display of salads and cakes is the London original - communal tables behind it, and a deli counter that shaped how a generation of home cooks eat.

restaurants.name: Coal Office
restaurants.whyGo: Assaf Granit's kitchen in a converted coal office at Coal Drops Yard, built around an open grill and a room designed by Tom Dixon.

restaurants.name: Berber & Q
restaurants.whyGo: A railway arch built around charcoal and smoke - lamb shawarma and cauliflower off the same grill, in a room that gets very loud very quickly.

restaurants.name: Em Sherif at Harrods
restaurants.address: Harrods, 87 135 Brompton Rd, London SW1X 7XL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The Beirut group's London outpost inside Harrods - a set Lebanese menu served in sequence rather than a mezze free-for-all.

restaurants.name: Maroush
restaurants.whyGo: Opened on Edgware Road in 1981 and effectively established the street as London's Lebanese quarter - still the reference point for everything that followed.

restaurants.name: Cafe Helen
restaurants.address: 105A Edgware Rd, Tyburnia, London W2 2HX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: An Edgware Road institution that comes into its own long after everywhere else has shut.
restaurants.opNote: Late-night trading is the point - it is a different place at midnight than at lunch.

restaurants.name: Ranoush Juice
restaurants.address: 43 Edgware Rd, Tyburnia, London W2 2JE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Rough, quick and mostly takeaway - the shawarma queue out of the door late on a weekend is an Edgware Road fixture in its own right.

restaurants.name: Maramia Cafe
restaurants.whyGo: Serving Palestinian and Arabic home cooking in west London since 2005, long before anyone was writing guides to it.

restaurants.name: Hiba Express
restaurants.whyGo: Family-run, generous and cheap - the lunch counter people in Holborn actually queue at rather than the one guidebooks send them to.

restaurants.name: Balady
restaurants.whyGo: Hummus treated as a dish rather than a dip - served warm, in a bowl, as the meal itself.

restaurants.name: Meza
restaurants.address: 34 Trinity Rd, Tooting Bec, London SW17 7RE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A tiny Tooting room where the mezze arrives faster than the table can clear it, at prices that explain the permanent queue.

restaurants.name: Common Breads
restaurants.address: 110 Buckingham Palace Rd, London SW1W 9SA, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Flatbreads and manakish straight out of the oven - a bakery counter rather than a restaurant, and cited by more guides than most restaurants here.

restaurants.name: Lebo Lebanese Grill
restaurants.whyGo: Cash only, mostly takeaway, and a late-night queue for the chicken that tells you everything about how good it is.
restaurants.opNote: Cash only. The queue builds late rather than at dinner time.

restaurants.name: Beit El Zaytoun
restaurants.address: 15-17 Barretts Green Rd, London NW10 7AE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Founded in 2016 by Ayman Assi as a small piece of Lebanon in northwest London, with a garden that does most of the work in summer.

restaurants.name: Berut Bistro
restaurants.whyGo: A small comfortable Lebanese room on Paddington Street - the neighbourhood version rather than the Edgware Road spectacle.

restaurants.name: Palmyra's Kitchen
restaurants.whyGo: Tucked round the back of Finsbury Park station, cooking across Lebanon and Syria - hidden in plain sight next to the bus stands.

restaurants.name: Ta'mini Lebanese Bakery
restaurants.whyGo: All-day manakish and fatayer from a husband-and-wife team, Ali from north Lebanon and Nermin from Beirut - opened in the first lockdown and has been expanding since.

restaurants.name: Al-Jabal Bakery
restaurants.address: F01, Acton Business Centre, School Rd, London NW10 6TD, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Twenty years of made-to-order mana'eesh in Acton - spinach and cheese, or lahem beajin - and a weekend queue drawn from across west London.

restaurants.name: Zeit & Za'atar
restaurants.whyGo: Za'atar manakish and vegetarian Levantine plates in Ealing, a long way from where the guides usually look.

restaurants.name: Fairuz
restaurants.whyGo: A long-running Marylebone Lebanese where the mezze arrives in waves and nobody is rushed out.

restaurants.name: Green Valley
restaurants.address: 36-37 Upper Berkeley St, London W1H 5QF, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Part supermarket, part counter, part patisserie - the Edgware Road institution people shop in and eat at in the same trip.

restaurants.name: Sohaila
restaurants.whyGo: Lebanese sharing plates against a hundred-plus natural wine list - and it is run by Fat Macy's, a social enterprise that helps Londoners move out of hostels into their own homes.

restaurants.name: Freej Swaileh
restaurants.whyGo: One of the very few Kuwaiti kitchens in London - machboos and kabsa rather than the Levantine mezze everywhere else does.

restaurants.name: T by Tamara
restaurants.whyGo: London's only fatteh bar, from Tamara Al Saadi - Palestinian and Jordanian cooking served as brunch, with the cakes doing serious work.

restaurants.name: Rovi
restaurants.address: 59 Wells Street, Fitzrovia, 59-65 Wells St, London W1A 3AE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The Ottolenghi group's fermentation-and-fire room, where vegetables go on the grill and get the treatment meat usually gets.

restaurants.name: Pilpel
restaurants.whyGo: The City lunch falafel - fast, consistent and vegetarian by default across a handful of sites.

restaurants.name: Hoxton Beach Falafel
restaurants.address: Whitecross St, Market Estate, London EC1Y 8JH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A market stall that has been frying falafel to order for years, and is on more London falafel lists than most sit-down restaurants.

restaurants.name: Magic Falafel
restaurants.address: Unit 312-313 Camden Lock Market, London NW1 8AH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Entirely vegan, fried fresh to order from 100 per cent ground chickpeas - trading in Camden Market since 2013.

restaurants.name: Falafel Zaki Zaki
restaurants.whyGo: A Palestinian-run stall doing generously filled wraps for the price of a coffee.

restaurants.name: Falafel & Shawarma
restaurants.address: 27 Camberwell Church St, London SE5 8TR, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Homemade falafel, hummus, chillies and salad in a flatbread, made to order in Camberwell.

restaurants.name: Hummus Bar
restaurants.address: 82 Golders Green Rd, London NW11 8LN, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Modelled on the hummus places of Tel Aviv, where a bowl of hummus is lunch rather than a side - the toppings list runs from oriental beef to sloppy joe.

restaurants.name: Kiln
restaurants.whyGo: Everything comes off wood and charcoal along a single counter - sit at the bar and the short rib curry is cooked in front of you.
restaurants.opNote: Counter seats are walk-in only and the wait is real. Tables can be booked.

restaurants.name: AngloThai
restaurants.whyGo: Thai cooking built on British seasonal produce rather than imported substitutes - the idea is in the name and it earned a Michelin star.

restaurants.name: Kolae
restaurants.whyGo: Southern Thai grilling from the Kiln team - a different regional tradition again, built around charcoal and coconut.

restaurants.name: Plaza Khao Gaeng
restaurants.address: 103-105 New Oxford St, London WC1A 1DB, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A khao gaeng shop - curries ladled over rice from a counter display - inside Arcade, and one of the few in London doing the format properly.

restaurants.name: Singburi
restaurants.address: Unit 7, Montacute Yards, 185‑186 Shoreditch High St, London E1 6HU, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A cult room where the specials board is the menu that matters and the cooking is uncompromising about heat.
restaurants.opNote: The specials change constantly - ask what is on rather than ordering from the printed menu.

restaurants.name: Farang
restaurants.whyGo: A north London room doing modern Thai with none of the timidity that usually comes with a neighbourhood address.

restaurants.name: The Begging Bowl
restaurants.whyGo: Jane Alty trained under David Thompson and cooks northern Thai in Peckham - small plates meant to be ordered across the table.

restaurants.name: Som Saa
restaurants.whyGo: Started as a London Fields pop-up and became the room that made regional Thai a London category - back in Time Out's top twenty after a kitchen fire.

restaurants.name: Smoking Goat
restaurants.address: 64 Shoreditch High St, London E1 6JJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Thai drinking food and live-fire cooking in a room that behaves like a bar - the sibling to Kiln and just as loud.

restaurants.name: Supawan
restaurants.whyGo: Understated, consistently good and near King's Cross - the Thai restaurant people return to rather than tick off.

restaurants.name: Khao So-i
restaurants.whyGo: Named for the northern Thai coconut curry noodle it is built around - the newest room on these lists and already on all of them.

restaurants.name: Kruk
restaurants.whyGo: A Bib Gourmand in Peckham - the value end of serious Thai cooking rather than the tasting-menu end.

restaurants.name: Esarn Kheaw
restaurants.whyGo: One of the longest-running Isaan kitchens in London, cooking the food of northeast Thailand long before anyone in Soho did.

restaurants.name: 101 Thai Kitchen
restaurants.whyGo: A west London standby that keeps turning up on lists compiled by people who eat a lot of Thai food.

restaurants.name: Miga
restaurants.whyGo: A family-run kitchen that moved from New Malden to Hackney in 2024 and was named Time Out's best restaurant in London - the yughwe beef tartare with crisp Asian pear is the dish everyone writes about.
restaurants.signals: Time Out best restaurant in London

restaurants.name: Jin Go Gae
restaurants.address: 272 Burlington Rd, New Malden KT3 4NL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Real charcoal rather than gas, which is why it is the purist's choice in a town full of Korean grills.

restaurants.name: Sorabol
restaurants.address: 180 High St, New Malden KT3 4ES, UK
