restaurants.whyGo: Twenty years on New Malden high street, where the owner will still tell you the right ratio of lettuce, garlic, leek and kimchi to build a wrap.

restaurants.name: K-Town BBQ
restaurants.address: 1st, 23 Blagdon Rd, New Malden KT3 4AH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: London's first all-you-can-eat Korean barbecue - industrial room, fixed price, and built for a table that intends to stay a while.
restaurants.opNote: Buffet format at a fixed price. Service charge is added on top.

restaurants.name: Imone
restaurants.address: Imone, BBQ, 171 High St, New Malden KT3 4BH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A small family-run room on New Malden high street, strong on seafood and with halal chicken options that most Korean kitchens do not offer.

restaurants.name: Chick and Beers
restaurants.whyGo: Family-owned, double-fried, and widely held to be the best Korean fried chicken in London - in the middle of New Malden's Koreatown rather than in town.

restaurants.name: CheeMc
restaurants.address: 32 Great Windmill St, London W1D 7LR, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Honey butter powder on double-fried chicken - the most-cited Korean fried chicken in central London.

restaurants.name: Sagye
restaurants.address: Ground Floor, Orion Point, 7 Crews St, London E14 3TU, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The warmer, slower side of Canary Wharf - kimchi jjigae portioned out between bowls for a big table, which is not how that estate usually eats.

restaurants.name: Olle
restaurants.whyGo: Table grills in the middle of Soho, so the New Malden format without the forty-minute train.

restaurants.name: Mukbap
restaurants.whyGo: Entirely vegan Korean cooking - a category that barely exists in London - served with the warmth of a family kitchen.

restaurants.name: Naru
restaurants.whyGo: A Shaftesbury Avenue standby whose dak twigim - crisp fried chicken bites with a choice of sauces - is the order.

restaurants.name: Seoul Bird
restaurants.whyGo: Judy Joo and Andrew Atkins soy-brine the chicken for a day before double-frying it - a counter format rather than a sit-down room.

restaurants.name: Jinjuu
restaurants.address: 15 Kingly St, Carnaby, London W1F 9BP, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Judy Joo's Soho room - the one that put modern Korean cooking on a central London street rather than a suburban high street.

restaurants.name: Tongdak
restaurants.address: 95A Kingston Rd, New Malden KT3 3PA, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A New Malden chicken specialist that trades almost entirely on the Korean community's own recommendation rather than on guides.

restaurants.name: Kol
restaurants.whyGo: Santiago Lastra cooks Mexican technique using British ingredients - no imported produce, which is the constraint the whole menu is built on.

restaurants.name: Santo Remedio
restaurants.whyGo: Edson and Natalie Diaz-Fuentes cook the dishes most London Mexicans skip - mole negro, soft shell crab tacos, and guacamole topped with grasshopper.
restaurants.signals: 5 consensus domains - the highest of any Mexican venue here

restaurants.name: Cavita
restaurants.whyGo: Time Out's pick for the best Mexican in London - the tacos get the headlines but the point is the dishes nobody else in London cooks.

restaurants.name: El Pastor
restaurants.whyGo: Al pastor carved off the trompo, in a railway-arch room that has been the default London taqueria for years.

restaurants.name: Tacos Padre
restaurants.address: The Borough Market Kitchen Padre, Winchester Walk, Jubilee, London SE1 9AG, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Corn nixtamalised on site and tortillas pressed to order at a Borough Market counter - the detail most taquerias skip.

restaurants.name: Sonora Taqueria
restaurants.address: 208 Stoke Newington High St, London N16 7HU, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Flour tortillas rather than corn, because that is what northern Sonora eats - a regional distinction nowhere else in London bothers with.

restaurants.name: Homies on Donkeys
restaurants.address: 686 High Rd Leytonstone, Bushwood, London E11 3AA, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Leytonstone taco counter that built a following on the strength of the tacos alone, with no room and no marketing to speak of.

restaurants.name: Cometa
restaurants.whyGo: Mexican seafood specifically - tostadas, ceviche and aguachile rather than the meat-led menu everywhere else runs.

restaurants.name: Ixchel
restaurants.whyGo: A Chelsea room that leans as hard on mezcal and the bar as on the kitchen.

restaurants.name: Zapote
restaurants.whyGo: Part of the east London Mexican wave that has moved the centre of gravity away from the west end entirely.

restaurants.name: Comalera
restaurants.address: Unit 31, Crate, 35 St James St, London E17 7FY, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Walthamstow stall pressing its own tortillas - the cheapest serious tacos on any of these lists.

restaurants.name: La Chingada
restaurants.address: 12 Rotherhithe New Rd, London SE16 2AA, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Al pastor, suadero, carnitas, chorizo and baja prawn - a southeast London taqueria that regulars rate above anything in zone 1.

restaurants.name: Mestizo
restaurants.whyGo: A long-running mezcaleria and dining room - the tequila and mezcal list is the reason to sit at the bar rather than a table.

restaurants.name: Addie's Thai
restaurants.whyGo: Trading since 1987 and packed for more than three decades - Bangkok street food in a room that never needed to reinvent itself.

restaurants.name: Nipa Thai
restaurants.address: First Floor, of, Lancaster Terrace, London W2 2TY, UK
restaurants.whyGo: One of the first Thai restaurants in London to charge what the French and Italian rooms charged - plush, polished, and still doing it.

restaurants.name: Khun Pakin Thai
restaurants.whyGo: Thai food out of a pub kitchen, which in London usually means a bad green curry - here it means fierce Isaan cooking.

restaurants.name: Paolina Thai
restaurants.address: 181 King's Cross Rd, London WC1X 9BZ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A dependable King's Cross room for a solo lunch or a low-key dinner, at prices that have not caught up with the neighbourhood.

restaurants.name: Patara Thai Wimbledon
restaurants.address: 18 High Street Wimbledon, London SW19 5DX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Curries worth the trip and a terrace that makes it a summer booking rather than a winter one.

restaurants.name: Flavour Hubb
restaurants.whyGo: Inside a racquets club, which is exactly the sort of address nobody would find on purpose - and the Thai food is among the most comforting in London.

restaurants.name: Jin-Da Thai
restaurants.whyGo: Northern Thai cooking on a Hammersmith side street, and the room Thai Londoners send people to rather than the ones in Soho.

restaurants.name: Mexican Seoul
restaurants.address: Bow Wharf, 221 Grove Rd., London E3 5SN, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Ashley Chipchase went from a Brick Lane street stall to a canalside room near Victoria Park in 2023, and the Korean-Mexican pairing turned out to be more than a gimmick.

restaurants.name: Assa
restaurants.whyGo: The budae jjigae - army stew - is the order, and it is among the best in London in a room that spends nothing on looking the part.

restaurants.name: Calong
restaurants.address: 35 Stoke Newington Church St, London N16 0NX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Chef-owner Joo Won runs a blackboard menu that puts subtle Korean seasoning through European cooking - a bistro rather than a small-plates repeat.

restaurants.name: Chung'dam
restaurants.whyGo: Named for Seoul's Cheongdam-dong and priced accordingly - the three-tiered pyeonbaek steam box of prawns, mussels and brisket is the thing to order.

restaurants.name: Seoul Matjib
restaurants.address: 74 Burlington Rd, New Malden KT3 4NU, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Tteokbokki with exactly the right chew, served without ceremony - the New Malden room people go to when they want feeding rather than impressing.

restaurants.name: Cake & Bingsoo
restaurants.address: 39 High St, New Malden KT3 4BY, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Bingsoo - shaved milk ice piled with fruit, ice cream and syrup - built for hot weather and shared between a table.

restaurants.name: Korean Grill Kensington
restaurants.whyGo: Tabletop grills at every table on the corner of Courtfield Road - it sits under the Millennium Gloucester but has its own entrance and none of the hotel-restaurant feel.

restaurants.name: Guacamoles
restaurants.whyGo: Hand-pressed tortillas dipped in birria juice before they hit the griddle, from a stall in Rye Lane Market.

restaurants.name: Taca Tacos
restaurants.address: Deptford Market Yard, London SE8 4BX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Six-hour beef birria and crisp baja fish tacos out of a Deptford railway arch, with margaritas to match.

restaurants.name: Speedboat Bar
restaurants.whyGo: Built to feel like a late-night Bangkok Chinatown canteen, with pool tables, and curries good enough that it was ranked the fourth best restaurant in London.
restaurants.signals: Time Out 50 Best Restaurants in London, number 4

restaurants.name: Chet's
restaurants.whyGo: Thai flavours through an American diner - an LA-inspired hotel room where the bar snacks and the drinks are doing as much work as the kitchen.

restaurants.name: Rabieng Thai
restaurants.whyGo: A long-standing Upper Street room near the Almeida, with generous portions and a BYOB policy that makes it cheaper again.
restaurants.opNote: BYOB - worth knowing before you order drinks.

restaurants.name: Pochawa Grill
restaurants.whyGo: A neon-pink Korean pub format dropped into Chinatown - you grill at the table and the room is built for a night rather than a meal.

restaurants.name: Jikoni
restaurants.whyGo: Ravinder Bhogal cooks across her Kenyan, Indian and British background without picking one - Ottolenghi called it the restaurant he wished he had opened.

restaurants.name: Oudh 1722
restaurants.whyGo: Two-Michelin-star chef Aktar Islam cooking the Awadhi food of Lucknow - biryanis and kebabs - across three floors of a Victorian townhouse near London Bridge.

restaurants.name: Corrochio's
restaurants.whyGo: Founder Daniel grew up in Guadalajara and trained in the Yucatan - the cooking is regional, and the cocktail bar runs long after the kitchen stops.

restaurants.name: Kitchen Table
restaurants.whyGo: Two Michelin stars cooked at a horseshoe counter with no menu given out in advance - you are told each course as it is put in front of you.

restaurants.name: Da Terra
restaurants.whyGo: Two stars inside a converted Bethnal Green town hall - Brazilian and Italian threads running through a fixed menu.

restaurants.name: Trivet
restaurants.whyGo: Two stars from a chef and a master sommelier working as equals - the wine list is the other half of the proposition, not an accessory.

restaurants.name: Row on 5
restaurants.whyGo: Jason Atherton's flagship, named for the 'refinement of work' - Spencer Metzger cooks British produce with a French hand, down to turbot with its own liver in the sauce.

restaurants.name: The Cocochine
restaurants.whyGo: Larry Jayasekara cooking inside a Mayfair townhouse owned by the gallerist behind Hamiltons - the art on the walls is the collection, not decoration.
restaurants.signals: La Liste Opening of the Year

restaurants.name: Lilibet's
restaurants.whyGo: Ross Shonhan went from exec chef at Nobu to founding Bone Daddies, and has now opened a full-dress Mayfair seafood room - an unusual arc.

restaurants.name: Frog by Adam Handling
restaurants.whyGo: A Michelin-starred tasting menu built around zero waste - trimmings from one course become the next, and it is stated rather than hidden.

restaurants.name: Chez Bruce
restaurants.whyGo: A Michelin star overlooking Wandsworth Common rather than a west end street - the definitive London argument that fine dining does not need a postcode.

restaurants.name: Trinity
restaurants.whyGo: Clapham Old Town's Michelin star, with a more relaxed room upstairs - the same kitchen at two different prices.

restaurants.name: One Club Row
restaurants.whyGo: Hidden up a staircase above a busy Shoreditch pub - pork schnitzel with gorgonzola and mustard, and a rice pudding creme brulee to finish.
restaurants.signals: 3 consensus domains - joint highest in the general pass

restaurants.name: Tollington's
restaurants.whyGo: Ed McIlroy of Four Legs took over an old Finsbury Park chip shop and put a 25-dish Iberian small-plates menu in it, smoked eel omelette included.

restaurants.name: Perilla
restaurants.address: 1-3 Green Lanes, Newington Green, London N16 9BS, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Newington Green room that has quietly been one of the best neighbourhood restaurants in London for years, and is back in the Top 100.

restaurants.name: Planque
restaurants.whyGo: Built around a members' wine cellar you can drink from - the food follows the bottle rather than the other way round.

restaurants.name: Brawn
restaurants.whyGo: One of the rooms that brought natural wine to London, on Columbia Road, and back in the Top 100 after more than a decade.

restaurants.name: Dorian
restaurants.whyGo: A Notting Hill butcher's shop turned bistro where the beef and the wine list are doing the talking.

restaurants.name: Ikoyi
restaurants.whyGo: Two Michelin stars and a menu that uses West African pantry ingredients - grains, peppers, fermentation - without presenting itself as a heritage restaurant.
restaurants.signals: Two Michelin stars; highest-scoring name in the general-excellence pass

restaurants.name: Chishuru
restaurants.address: 3 Great Titchfield St., London W1W 8AX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Adejoké Bakare became the first Black female chef in Britain to hold a Michelin star, cooking the food of west Africa on a fixed menu.

restaurants.name: Akoko
restaurants.whyGo: A Michelin-starred tasting menu drawing on the cooking of Nigeria, Ghana and Senegal, with a grill and a clay oven at the centre of it.

restaurants.name: Chuku's
restaurants.whyGo: Nigerian food served as tapas by a brother-and-sister team - the format is the idea, and it makes an unfamiliar menu easy to order from.

restaurants.name: Akara
restaurants.address: Arch 208, 18 Stoney St, London SE1 9AD, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Named after the black-eyed bean fritter it is built around, from the Chishuru team - the casual counterpart to the starred room.

restaurants.name: Master Wei
restaurants.whyGo: Hand-pulled biang biang noodles and Xi'an street food near Russell Square, from the team behind Xi'an Impression.

restaurants.name: Osteria Vibrato
restaurants.whyGo: A compact Soho osteria from Charlie Mellor with a 300-bin list of natural and biodynamic wine - Italian at its backbone, French alongside it.

restaurants.name: Bouchon Racine
restaurants.address: Upstairs, 66 Cowcross St, London EC1M 6BP, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Henry Harris cooking unapologetic French bourgeois food above a Farringdon pub - and named the best restaurant in the UK at the 2026 National Restaurant Awards.
restaurants.signals: National Restaurant Awards, number 1 in the UK

restaurants.name: Camille
restaurants.whyGo: A small Borough bistro doing offal, terrines and the unfashionable half of the French repertoire properly.

restaurants.name: Casse-Croûte
restaurants.whyGo: Three dishes per course chalked on a board, a room the size of a front parlour, and no concession to anything but France.

restaurants.name: The French House
restaurants.whyGo: The Soho pub that was the Free French headquarters in the war, with a small dining room above it and beer served only in halves downstairs.

restaurants.name: Otto's
restaurants.address: 182 Gray's Inn Rd, London WC1X 8EW, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Canard à la presse carved and pressed at the table - one of the last places in London performing classical French service as theatre.

restaurants.name: 64 Goodge Street
restaurants.address: 64 Goodge Street, Greater, 64 Goodge St, Greater, London W1T 4NF, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Fitzrovia brasserie from the Woodhead group doing the format straight - steak frites, a long bar, and late service.

restaurants.name: Pique-Nique
restaurants.whyGo: The Casse-Croûte team in a former park pavilion in Bermondsey, built around rotisserie chicken and a short set menu.

restaurants.name: Les 2 Garçons
restaurants.whyGo: A Crouch End neighbourhood bistro that would pass without comment in Lyon and stands out considerably in north London.

restaurants.name: Paulette
restaurants.whyGo: A Maida Vale bistro doing short, seasonal French menus for a neighbourhood not overrun with them.

restaurants.name: La Poule au Pot
restaurants.whyGo: Trading since the 1960s on coq au vin, beef bourguignon and candlelight - the most reliably romantic dining room in London by some distance.

restaurants.name: Barrafina Dean Street
restaurants.whyGo: No bookings, counter only, and a Michelin star - you queue, you sit where you are put, and the plancha is a foot away.
restaurants.opNote: Walk-in only. The queue is shortest at opening and after 2pm.

restaurants.name: José
restaurants.whyGo: José Pizarro's standing-room sherry bar on Bermondsey Street - a handful of stools, a lot of jamón, and no way to book.

restaurants.name: Morito
restaurants.whyGo: The small, loud offshoot of Moro next door - a dozen seats at the counter and a menu that changes constantly.

restaurants.name: Sabor
restaurants.whyGo: Nieves Barragán Mohacho cooks her mother's Basque and Galician repertoire downstairs and roasts suckling pig in a wood oven upstairs.

restaurants.name: Copita
restaurants.whyGo: A narrow Soho bar built for standing, small plates and sherry by the copita it is named after.

restaurants.name: Dehesa
restaurants.address: 25 Ganton St, Carnaby, London W1F 9BP, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A corner site off Carnaby Street running Spanish and Italian small plates side by side, which is rarer than it sounds.

restaurants.name: Bar Kroketa
restaurants.address: 21 Beak St, Carnaby, London W1F 9RR, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Built around the croqueta and not much else - a single-dish bar, done properly.

restaurants.name: ALTA
restaurants.address: Ground Floor, Kingly Ct, Carnaby, London W1B 5PW, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Basque live-fire cooking in Soho - everything routed through the grill, including the vegetables.

restaurants.name: Ember Yard
restaurants.whyGo: Charcoal and smoke run through the whole menu, from the meat to the ice cream.

restaurants.name: Escocesa
restaurants.address: 67 Stoke Newington Church St, London N16 0AR, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Scottish seafood cooked the Spanish way in Stoke Newington - the name is the whole idea.

restaurants.name: Mangal 2
restaurants.address: 4 Stoke Newington Rd, London N16 7XN, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The Dirik brothers took over their father's Dalston ocakbaşı and turned it into one of the most inventive kitchens in London without moving the grill.

restaurants.name: Oklava
restaurants.whyGo: Selin Kiazim cooking Turkish-Cypriot food as small plates - the pistachio-crusted lamb and the menemen are the reference points.

restaurants.name: Antepliler
restaurants.address: 43 Grand Parade, Green Lanes, Harringay Ladder, London N4 1AQ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Green Lanes cooking from Gaziantep, with a baklava counter that is the reason half the customers are there.

restaurants.name: Gökyüzü
restaurants.address: 26-28 Grand Parade, Green Lanes, Harringay Ladder, London N4 1LG, UK
restaurants.whyGo: An enormous Green Lanes grill house where the mixed kebab arrives on a platter built for four and feeds six.

restaurants.name: FM Mangal
restaurants.address: 54 Camberwell Church St, London SE5 8QZ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: South London's answer to Green Lanes - charcoal, lahmacun and no ceremony whatsoever.

restaurants.name: Köfteci Metin
restaurants.address: 553 Green Lanes, Harringay Ladder, London N8 0RL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Köfte and very little else, which is exactly why it is worth the trip up Green Lanes.

restaurants.name: The Mantl
restaurants.whyGo: Turkish cooking taken to Knightsbridge prices, themed around a family hearth - tradition and innovation on the same plate.

restaurants.name: Ishtar
restaurants.whyGo: A long-running Marylebone Turkish room with a mezze list built for a table that wants to stay put.

restaurants.name: Le Bab
restaurants.address: Top Floor, Kingly Ct, Carnaby St, Carnaby, London W1B 5PW, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Kebabs rebuilt with restaurant technique - the format is familiar and almost nothing else about it is.

restaurants.name: Durak Tantuni
restaurants.address: 390 W Green Rd, London N15 3PX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Tantuni - finely chopped beef griddled and rolled in flatbread - which almost nowhere else in London serves.

restaurants.name: Cây Tre
restaurants.whyGo: Hiếu Bùi is treated as the godfather of Vietnamese food in London, and the bone marrow phở is the bowl that argument rests on.
restaurants.signals: Time Out best Vietnamese in London

restaurants.name: Sông Quê Café
restaurants.whyGo: The Kingsland Road institution that made the street synonymous with phở - strip lighting, fast turnover, enormous menu.

restaurants.name: Viet Grill
restaurants.whyGo: The smarter end of Kingsland Road, from the Cây Tre group, with a wine list someone has actually thought about.

restaurants.name: Hoa Sen
restaurants.whyGo: The roast duck served in lettuce leaves with mango is the dish to order and the reason to cross Covent Garden for it.

restaurants.name: Bánh Bánh
restaurants.whyGo: A family recipe book turned into a Peckham restaurant, run by the grandchildren of the cook it came from.

restaurants.name: Banh Mi Kêu
restaurants.whyGo: Bánh mì made to order rather than pre-wrapped, which is the whole difference.

restaurants.name: OPSO
restaurants.whyGo: Greek small plates reworked with restaurant technique - the room most responsible for London taking modern Greek cooking seriously.

restaurants.name: Lemonia
restaurants.address: 89 Regent's Park Rd, London NW1 8UY, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Primrose Hill taverna that has been feeding the same families for decades - big, noisy and entirely unbothered by fashion.

restaurants.name: Mazi
restaurants.whyGo: Notting Hill Greek that treats the classics as a starting point rather than a checklist, with a garden at the back.

restaurants.name: Meraki
restaurants.address: 80 Great Titchfield St., London W1W 7QT, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A large Fitzrovia room from the Roka and Zuma group, doing Greek at that group's usual volume.

restaurants.name: Kima
restaurants.whyGo: Whole fish and Greek seafood cooking treated at fine-dining level, which almost nothing else in London does.

restaurants.name: Zylia
restaurants.whyGo: A Queen's Park neighbourhood Greek doing small plates well enough to draw people from outside the postcode.

restaurants.name: Oma
restaurants.whyGo: Upstairs from its own more casual sibling at Borough Market, cooking Greek food over fire at serious prices and justifying them.

restaurants.name: Maza
restaurants.whyGo: Greek mezze at Mayfair scale, from the OPSO team.

restaurants.name: Legado
restaurants.address: Unit 1C Montacute, Yards, London E1 6HU, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Nieves Barragán Mohacho's second restaurant after Sabor, cooking regional Spanish food rarely seen this side of the Pyrenees - and it took a Michelin star within two years.

restaurants.name: Ibai
restaurants.whyGo: Fire-led Basque cooking and some of the best beef in the country, from the team behind Donostia - a tribute to the original Ibai in San Sebastián.

restaurants.name: Maresco
restaurants.whyGo: Spanish technique applied to Scottish seafood, on a daily specials board that changes with what lands.

restaurants.name: Lurra
restaurants.whyGo: Aged Galician beef and whole turbot over coals, from the Donostia team - the Basque asador format done properly.

restaurants.name: Pizarro
restaurants.whyGo: The sit-down sibling to José a few doors up - same chef, tables instead of stools, and you can book.

restaurants.name: Parrillan
restaurants.whyGo: You get your own small charcoal grill at the table and cook the skewers yourself - a format nothing else in London offers.

restaurants.name: Salt Yard
restaurants.whyGo: One of the rooms that started London's small-plates habit, still doing courgette flowers stuffed with goat's cheese and honey.

restaurants.name: The Tapas Room
restaurants.address: New Acres, 25A Swandon Way, London SW18 1EJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Small, loud south London tapas bars where the wine list is as much the point as the plates.

restaurants.name: Pyro
restaurants.whyGo: Yiannis Mexis' first restaurant, built around an open fire - potato pittas with smoked aubergine and spiced feta before anything else.

restaurants.name: Vori
restaurants.address: 120 Holland Park Ave, London W11 4UA, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The only wine list in London built entirely on indigenous Greek varieties, in a Holland Park Avenue taverna with tables on the pavement.

restaurants.name: Zephyr
restaurants.whyGo: From the Pachamama group, on Portobello Road - one of the most photographed rooms in west London, and the cooking holds up.

restaurants.name: The Life Goddess
restaurants.whyGo: Part deli, part taverna - you can buy the cheese you just ate, which is most of the appeal.

restaurants.name: Tsiakkos & Charcoal
restaurants.whyGo: A Maida Vale back-street Cypriot grill that has not changed in decades and has no intention of doing so.

restaurants.name: Andy's Taverna
restaurants.whyGo: An old-school Camden taverna doing meze for large tables at prices that explain its longevity.

restaurants.name: Enfes Ocakbaşı
restaurants.whyGo: A brightly lit Green Lanes canteen with nothing to look at but the grill, which is the entire point - adana, shish, liver and chops, all cooked properly.

restaurants.name: Motorino
restaurants.whyGo: Luke Ahearne and Stevie Parle call it London-Italian rather than Italian - the distinction is the point, and the cooking earns it.

restaurants.name: Bonheur by Matt Abé
restaurants.whyGo: Matt Abé left Restaurant Gordon Ramsay to open his first solo room, and it took two Michelin stars within three months - about as fast as that has happened in London.
restaurants.signals: Two Michelin stars, awarded three months after opening

restaurants.name: Teal by Sally Abé
restaurants.whyGo: Sally Abé's first solo restaurant, named after the game bird rather than the colour - British ingredients, British food history, and a stated commitment to the people who supply it.

restaurants.name: Impala
restaurants.whyGo: Meedu Saad left the top job at Kiln to cook his own history - Egyptian heritage crossed with the Cypriot kebab houses of north London he grew up around.

restaurants.name: Med Salleh Viet
restaurants.whyGo: Grilled Vietnamese street food and phở, run halal by the couple behind Med Salleh Kopitiam - a combination almost nothing else in London offers.

restaurants.name: Duck & Waffle
restaurants.whyGo: Forty floors up and open around the clock - the only place in London where you can watch the sun come up over the City with a plate in front of you.
restaurants.signature: Duck egg, confit duck leg and waffle
restaurants.opNote: Open 24 hours. Sunrise and late-night slots are the ones worth planning for.

restaurants.name: Aqua Shard
restaurants.address: Level 31, The Shard, 31 St Thomas St, London SE1 9RY, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Floor-to-ceiling glass on the 31st floor of the Shard, with the atrium running up three storeys above the dining room.

restaurants.name: OXO Tower Restaurant
restaurants.address: Barge House St, London SE1 9PH, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A long terrace on the eighth floor looking straight across the Thames at St Paul's - the classic London river view, and it has been that for thirty years.

restaurants.name: Darwin Brasserie
restaurants.address: 1, Level 36, Sky Garden Walk, London EC3M 8AF, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Inside the Sky Garden's glass dome at the top of the Walkie Talkie, surrounded by planting rather than just glass.
restaurants.opNote: Sky Garden entry is free but ticketed; a restaurant booking gets you in without one.

restaurants.name: Berners Tavern
restaurants.whyGo: A vast Edwardian ballroom with every inch of wall covered in framed pictures - probably the most photographed dining room in London.

restaurants.name: Sessions Arts Club
restaurants.whyGo: A crumbling former courthouse left deliberately unrestored - peeling plaster, enormous windows, and no attempt to make it look finished.

restaurants.name: Julie's
restaurants.whyGo: A warren of small rooms and alcoves in Holland Park, named by Prix Versailles among the most beautiful restaurants in the world after its relaunch.

restaurants.name: Bob Bob Ricard
restaurants.address: 1 Upper James St, London W1F 9DF, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Booth-only, art deco throughout, and a Press for Champagne button at every table - the gimmick that launched a thousand photographs.

restaurants.name: Brasserie of Light
restaurants.address: 400 Oxford St, Duke St, London W1A 1AB, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A crystal-encrusted Damien Hirst pegasus hangs over the room inside Selfridges - subtlety is not the objective.

restaurants.name: Brooklands
restaurants.address: The Peninsula, 1 Grosvenor Pl, London SW1X 7HJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Claude Bosi cooking on the roof of the Peninsula, in a room themed on British motor racing and aviation, looking over Hyde Park Corner.

restaurants.name: SUSHISAMBA
restaurants.whyGo: An orange tree growing through an open-air terrace on the 39th floor - the highest outdoor dining in the City, with the lift ride as part of the experience.

restaurants.name: Shanghai Me
restaurants.context: London Hilton on Park Lane, 28th floor
restaurants.address: Hilton on, 22 Park Ln, London W1K 1BE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Lacquered wood and 1930s glamour twenty-eight floors above Park Lane, looking down the length of Hyde Park.

restaurants.name: Forza Wine
restaurants.whyGo: A terrace on top of the National Theatre looking straight up the Thames - the best free view attached to a wine list in London.

restaurants.name: The Barbary
restaurants.whyGo: A horseshoe counter wrapped around an open grill in Neal's Yard, seating about twenty - you watch every plate being made.

restaurants.name: Din Tai Fung
restaurants.whyGo: Xiao long bao folded to eighteen pleats behind glass - the Taiwanese chain Ken Hom put in the New York Times' world top ten, and its first London site.
restaurants.opNote: Walk-in queues are long at peak. Centre Point is the larger site with a bar lounge.

restaurants.name: Mr Bao
restaurants.whyGo: Gua bao and Taiwanese small plates in Peckham, at a price that makes it a regular rather than a trip.

restaurants.name: Good Friend Chicken
restaurants.address: 14 Little Newport St, London WC2H 7JJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Taiwanese popcorn chicken fried to order in Chinatown - salt, pepper and fried basil, eaten standing up.

restaurants.name: Mambow
restaurants.whyGo: Abby Lee named it for her mother's bowls and cooks Malaysian food through an open kitchen, against low-intervention wine.
restaurants.signals: Time Out 50 Best Restaurants; Michelin Guide listed

restaurants.name: Normah's
restaurants.address: 23 25 Queensway market Inside, Queensway market, London W2 4QJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A Malaysian kitchen tucked inside a Queensway market building, cooking nasi lemak and rendang for people who grew up on them.

restaurants.name: Rasa Sayang
restaurants.whyGo: Hainanese chicken rice and char kway teow in Chinatown, at the volume and price of a hawker centre.

restaurants.name: Gopal's Corner
restaurants.whyGo: Roti canai clapped and folded to order, served with mutton, chicken or dhal curry - from the founder of Soho's Roti King.

restaurants.name: Donia
restaurants.address: 2.5, Top Floor, Kingly Ct, Carnaby St, Carnaby, London W1B 5PW, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Filipino sharing plates in Kingly Court with a European wine list behind them - the first Filipino room in London to take a Bib Gourmand.

restaurants.name: Belly Bistro
restaurants.whyGo: Part French bistro, part Filipino kitchen - the fish sauce profiteroles with salted caramel are the dish that explains the whole place.
restaurants.signals: Time Out 50 Best; Michelin Guide listed

restaurants.name: Zeret Kitchen
restaurants.whyGo: A family-run Camberwell room where everything arrives on one injera for the table to tear at - communal eating with no way to opt out of it.

restaurants.name: Queen of Sheba
restaurants.whyGo: A long-running Kentish Town Ethiopian with a vegetarian platter that converts people who came for the meat.

restaurants.name: Tasty Jerk
restaurants.whyGo: Four steel drums behind the counter smoking jerk chicken and pork belly - takeaway only, and worth the journey south for it.
restaurants.opNote: Takeaway only. There is nowhere to sit.

restaurants.name: Paradise Cove
restaurants.address: Brent Cove Drop-in Service, 27-29 Fairlight Ave, London NW10 8AL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Jerk cooked over pimento wood in northwest London, on a stretch that has been the centre of Caribbean London for decades.

restaurants.name: Hoppers
restaurants.whyGo: Hoppers, kothu and sambols from the JKS group - Sri Lankan and Tamil cooking that London had been filing under Indian for years.

restaurants.name: Berenjak
restaurants.whyGo: A Tehran hole-in-the-wall kabab house rebuilt in Soho - mahi, jujeh and torshi at a counter, from the JKS group.

restaurants.name: Patogh
restaurants.whyGo: A tiny room off Edgware Road where the flatbread comes out roughly the size of a sombrero and the kebabs are cooked over coals.

restaurants.name: Doma
restaurants.whyGo: Spasia Dinkovski reopened after Mystic Burek closed, and Doma - 'at home' in Macedonian - trades one day a week with a different proposition each Saturday.
restaurants.opNote: Saturdays only, and the format changes week to week - check before travelling.

restaurants.name: Granger & Co
restaurants.whyGo: Bill Granger brought Sydney brunch to London and the ricotta hotcakes have been on the menu ever since - the reason half of London eats avocado on toast.
restaurants.opNote: No bookings at weekend brunch at most sites.

restaurants.name: Milk
restaurants.whyGo: A Balham cafe that has topped London brunch lists for years without ever opening a second site.

restaurants.name: Rosina
restaurants.whyGo: Adam Byatt spent two decades building a modern British reputation and then opened an Italian restaurant on the corner of Wandsworth Common.

restaurants.name: Clio
restaurants.whyGo: A 2026 opening on Chiltern Street, and the newest of the Marylebone Greek rooms.

restaurants.name: All Roads
restaurants.whyGo: A Brixton residency that took a permanent site in May 2026, with a menu drawn from the founders' own heritage and travels.

restaurants.name: Vesper
restaurants.whyGo: Jackson Boxer on Exmouth Market with cold martinis and British comfort food - the 240g beef burger is limited and has been known to sell out in seconds.
restaurants.opNote: The burger is capped daily and goes almost immediately after service opens.
restaurants.signals: 5 new-openings domains - the highest of the pass

restaurants.name: 130 Primrose Hill
restaurants.address: 130 Regent's Park Rd, London NW1 8XL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A charity-led restaurant that recruits people with experience of homelessness and pays them through accredited training - with Monica Galetti as executive chef.
restaurants.opNote: Open all day, every day. 50 covers, with salads and sandwiches at lunch.

restaurants.name: Kinz
restaurants.address: 50 Notting Hill Gate, London W11 3JD, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A 1930s Lloyds Bank on Notting Hill Gate turned Lebanese brasserie - triple-height ground floor, a deli at the front and the wine room inside the old vault.

restaurants.name: No. Forty Nine
restaurants.address: 49-51 St John's Wood High St, London NW8 7NJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Morning pastries through to late European wine on St John's Wood High Street - the Cinder team running a bakery, a bistro and a wine bar out of one corner site.

restaurants.name: Tavern
restaurants.whyGo: The Restaurant St Barts team took over the old Nest site and brought part of their own kitchen brigade with them.

restaurants.name: Temaki Mayfair
restaurants.whyGo: The handroll bar that started in Brixton in 2021 and moved central - temaki made to order, plus crispy rice, wagyu sliders and sandos.

restaurants.name: The Sea, The Sea
restaurants.whyGo: The fishmonger that supplies Ikoyi and KOL, now with a 40-seat bistro above and a ten-seat seafood bar below - you can buy the fish on the way out.

restaurants.name: Appalachia
restaurants.whyGo: The cooking of the Appalachian mountains - cornbread madeleines, poussin with grits - from a chef who came out of Smoking Goat, at a counter wrapped round an open kitchen.

restaurants.name: Hon's BBQ
restaurants.context: above Crate Brewery, former Silo site
restaurants.address: First floor, Unit 7, The white building, Queen's Yard, London E9 5EN, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Man Hon Luk smokes Texan barbecue through Chinese and Asian seasoning, canalside in Hackney Wick in the room Silo used to occupy.

restaurants.name: Kiez Kebab
restaurants.whyGo: Berlin döner rather than London kebab - three options only, served in pide bread rather than wrapped, on Golborne Road.

restaurants.name: Kismet
restaurants.address: The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale St, London SE1 9AL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A meyhane in the style of Istanbul and north Cyprus, upstairs at The Globe - in the building used as Bridget Jones's flat in the films.

restaurants.name: Langosteria London
restaurants.whyGo: The Milan seafood group's first London site, inside the Old War Office - spaghetti with clams and sea urchin, and prices to match the address.

restaurants.name: Lokal
restaurants.whyGo: Modern Turkish cooking from the Fred Bakery and Faros team, with counter dining and a cocktail bar alongside 110 covers.

restaurants.name: Mour
restaurants.whyGo: All-day Mediterranean in Marylebone with a martini bar and a courtyard most people walking past would never know is there.

restaurants.name: Ornella
restaurants.whyGo: Milanese cooking on Wilton Way from the team behind Roman-influenced Lupa in Highbury - a butter-yellow corner site done simply.

restaurants.name: Sale e Pepe Mare
restaurants.whyGo: Ligurian coastal cooking at The Langham, carrying over the original Sale e Pepe's cacio e pepe finished tableside in a cheese wheel.
restaurants.signature: Bucatini cacio e pepe, finished in the wheel

restaurants.name: The Victory
restaurants.whyGo: Franklins on Lordship Lane relaunched under its original name, with British ingredient-led cooking pushed through a modern French bistro lens.

restaurants.name: Bar Etna
restaurants.whyGo: Joe Beddia of Pizzeria Beddia in Philadelphia partnered with Four Legs to open his only restaurant outside the United States - a New York and Philly pizza site crossed with an Italian neighbourhood bar.

restaurants.name: Prufrock Coffee
restaurants.whyGo: The Leather Lane shop that trained a generation of London baristas - it runs its own training centre, and most serious coffee people in the city passed through it.
restaurants.signals: 5 consensus domains - the highest of the coffee pass; named among the best in the UK 2026

restaurants.name: Monmouth Coffee Company
restaurants.whyGo: Roasting since 1978 and still the default answer to where to get coffee in London - the Borough Market shop has a queue out of the door most mornings.
restaurants.opNote: The Borough queue is longest at weekend market hours. Covent Garden is quieter.

restaurants.name: Kaffeine
restaurants.whyGo: Australian-run and one of the shops that brought antipodean coffee culture to London - the food counter is as good as the espresso.

restaurants.name: Origin Coffee Roasters
restaurants.whyGo: Roasted in Cornwall and poured in a clean, modern Shoreditch room - a favourite of the people who take this most seriously.

restaurants.name: The Attendant
restaurants.whyGo: Built inside a restored Victorian public lavatory, with the original porcelain urinals turned into the counter you sit at.

restaurants.name: WatchHouse
restaurants.whyGo: Started in a nineteenth-century watchman's hut on Bermondsey Street and has become the most polished coffee group in London.

restaurants.name: Ozone Coffee Roasters
restaurants.whyGo: A working roastery in the basement with a full kitchen above it - closer to an all-day restaurant than a coffee shop.

restaurants.name: Caravan
restaurants.whyGo: An all-day kitchen with its own roastery attached - the room most responsible for London's brunch-and-flat-white format.

restaurants.name: Workshop Coffee
restaurants.address: 32-34 New Cavendish St, London W1G 8UE, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A roaster's shop where the filter list changes constantly and the staff will talk you through it if you want.

restaurants.name: Rosslyn Coffee
restaurants.whyGo: A tiny City counter that consistently tops London coffee rankings and has almost nowhere to sit.

restaurants.name: Climpson & Sons
restaurants.whyGo: On Broadway Market since before the street became what it is now, roasting its own and still busiest on Saturdays.

restaurants.name: Redemption Roasters
restaurants.address: 84b Lamb's Conduit St, London WC1N 3LR, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The beans are roasted inside prisons by people the company then trains and employs on release - a coffee chain built entirely around reducing reoffending.

restaurants.name: Old Spike
restaurants.whyGo: A Peckham roastery that employs and trains people who have experienced homelessness - the coffee stands on its own, which is rather the point.

restaurants.name: Algerian Coffee Stores
restaurants.whyGo: Trading on Old Compton Street since 1887, selling beans over the counter with an espresso hatch and nowhere at all to sit.

restaurants.name: Catalyst
restaurants.address: 48 Gray's Inn Rd, Chancery Ln, London WC1X 8LT, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A pared-back Scandi room near Prufrock, and named among the best coffee shops in the UK for 2026.
restaurants.signals: Named among the best coffee shops in the UK 2026

restaurants.name: Carbon Kopi
restaurants.whyGo: Moved from New Zealand to Hammersmith in 2019 and has been on the national best-of lists ever since.
restaurants.signals: Named among the best coffee shops in the UK 2026

restaurants.name: Greenwich Market
restaurants.whyGo: A covered Georgian market where the food stalls rotate daily - Ethiopian, Persian, Indian, barbecue and churros within about thirty paces of each other.
restaurants.opNote: Stall line-up changes day to day. Busiest at weekends; some traders are weekend-only.

restaurants.name: Cutty Sark Street Food Market
restaurants.address: Coltman House, Welland St, London SE10 9DW, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Weekend-only stalls in Cutty Sark Gardens, right by the ship and the river - paella, souvlaki, Korean corn dogs and pizza.
restaurants.opNote: Friday to Sunday only. It does not trade midweek.

restaurants.name: Peninsula Restaurant
restaurants.style: Modern European with a river view
restaurants.address: 141-143 Greenwich S St, London SE10 8NX, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Floor-to-ceiling glass looking straight across the river at the Canary Wharf towers - the best dining-room view in southeast London and Michelin-recognised.

restaurants.name: Wandercrust
restaurants.address: The Pelton Arms, The Pelton Arms, 23-25 Pelton Rd, London SE10 9PQ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Proper Neapolitan bases in Greenwich, which the area has an unusual amount of for its size.

restaurants.name: Alhaji Suya
restaurants.whyGo: Suya - beef skewered, spiced with yaji and grilled over charcoal - which almost nowhere in this half of London does properly.

restaurants.name: Hullabaloo
restaurants.address: 10 Greenwich Church St, London SE10 9BJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: A permanent fixture in Greenwich Market rather than a rotating stall, doing vegetarian and vegan Indian street food.

restaurants.name: Champagne + Fromage
restaurants.address: 34 Greenwich Church St, London SE10 9BL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: French cheese, charcuterie and grower champagne by the glass - a small chain, but the Greenwich site sits right by the market.

restaurants.name: The Gun
restaurants.whyGo: A Grade II listed early nineteenth-century pub on the Thames at Coldharbour, looking across at the O2 - a genuine old building in an area that has almost none left.

restaurants.name: Berberè
restaurants.address: 154, The Street, Montfichet Rd, London E20 1EN, UK
restaurants.whyGo: An Italian chain that takes sourdough fermentation seriously, and routinely rated among the best pizza in London - not the sort of thing Stratford is assumed to have.

restaurants.name: The Cow
restaurants.address: 4, Chestnut Plaza, Montfichet Rd, London E20 1GL, UK
restaurants.whyGo: The sit-down alternative to the Westfield food court, with a terrace - which in Stratford is a genuinely short list.

restaurants.name: All Star Lanes
restaurants.whyGo: Fried chicken and mac and cheese inside a bowling alley - not a food destination, but the answer when the table includes teenagers.

restaurants.name: Smith's of Wapping
restaurants.whyGo: Fish served plainly and well, in a dining room looking straight at Tower Bridge - the view is the reason and the kitchen does not fight it.

restaurants.name: The Melusine
restaurants.address: Unit K, Ivory House, St Katharine Docks, E Smithfield, London E1W 1AT, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Fish brought up from the coast daily, on a dock full of moored boats - the most pleasant place to sit outside in this part of London.

restaurants.name: The Turk's Head
restaurants.whyGo: A neighbourhood bistro running French classics at prices that have not followed the postcode.

restaurants.name: Joia
restaurants.address: 15th Floor, 1 Electric Blvd, Nine Elms, London SW11 8BJ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Portuguese cooking fourteen floors up beside the Power Station, and one of very few serious Portuguese kitchens in London.

restaurants.name: Wright Brothers
restaurants.address: 26 Circus West Village, The Power Station, Nine Elms, London SW11 8EZ, UK
restaurants.whyGo: An oyster bar with fish arriving from Devon daily and a specials board that changes with the boat.

restaurants.name: Sticks'n'Sushi
restaurants.whyGo: A Danish-Japanese format that puts sushi and skewers on the same menu - reliable rather than remarkable, and useful when a table cannot agree.

restaurants.name: Bread Street Kitchen
restaurants.address: Circus Road South Turbine, Hall A, 1st Floor, The Power Station, Nine Elms, London SW11 8DD, UK
restaurants.whyGo: Gordon Ramsay's all-day format - a steak, a burger and a long opening span. The reliable option rather than the interesting one, and it turns up wherever a new development does.
restaurants.opNote: All-day service, which in a new development is often the only thing open between lunch and dinner.

restaurants.name: Toad Bakery
restaurants.whyGo: A Camberwell bakery that has been on every best-of list two years running, doing sandwiches and pastries out of a small shopfront.
restaurants.signals: 3 consensus domains; Good Food Guide 50 Best Bakeries

restaurants.name: E5 Bakehouse
restaurants.whyGo: Sourdough milled and baked under the London Fields arches, with a cafe attached and flour sold by the bag.
restaurants.signals: 3 consensus domains; Good Food Guide 50 Best Bakeries

restaurants.name: Chatsworth Bakehouse
restaurants.whyGo: Started as lockdown loaves and is now on the national fifty - the queue on a Saturday morning is the whole of Crystal Palace.
restaurants.signals: 3 consensus domains; Good Food Guide 50 Best Bakeries

restaurants.name: Arôme
restaurants.whyGo: Laminated croissants taken seriously, and a miso bacon escargot that has no business working as well as it does.

restaurants.name: Suba Bakery
restaurants.whyGo: On the national fifty two years running, and named for its lamination above anything else.
restaurants.signals: 3 consensus domains; Good Food Guide 50 Best Bakeries

restaurants.name: August Bakery
restaurants.signals: 3 consensus domains; Good Food Guide 50 Best Bakeries

restaurants.name: Pophams
restaurants.whyGo: Pastries at the counter and a small kitchen behind it, so it works as breakfast and as lunch.

restaurants.name: The Dusty Knuckle
restaurants.whyGo: Bread and sandwiches from a bakery that runs a training programme for young people facing barriers to work - the sandwich is famous on its own merits.

restaurants.name: Layla
restaurants.whyGo: A Portobello Road bakery doing wood-fired bread and pastries, and one of the few reasons to be at that end of the street on a weekday.

restaurants.name: Fortitude Bakehouse
restaurants.whyGo: A small Bloomsbury bakehouse a couple of minutes from Russell Square, which is a short list.

restaurants.name: Lily Vanilli
restaurants.whyGo: Open on Sundays for the Columbia Road flower market and largely closed the rest of the week - cakes as the reason, not the afterthought.
restaurants.opNote: Sunday-led, tied to the flower market. Check before travelling midweek.

restaurants.name: Violet Cakes
restaurants.whyGo: Claire Ptak's Hackney bakery - the one that made the royal wedding cake, and still a small shop selling cupcakes over a counter.

restaurants.name: Cédric Grolet at The Berkeley
restaurants.whyGo: Trompe-l'oeil fruit pastries from one of the most decorated patissiers working - the queue starts before opening and the good things sell out.
restaurants.opNote: Sells out early. The queue forms before the doors open.

restaurants.name: St John Bakery
restaurants.whyGo: The custard doughnut that every other London bakery has since tried to copy, sold from a Maltby Street arch.

restaurants.name: Gelupo
restaurants.whyGo: A side street off Piccadilly, opposite its own sibling restaurant, turning out gelato that changes with what is in season.

restaurants.name: Oddono's
restaurants.whyGo: The South Kensington original is still the one locals use, and the pistachio is the benchmark everyone else is measured against.

restaurants.name: Badiani
restaurants.whyGo: The Florence gelateria that brought its Buontalenti - an egg-and-cream recipe with a protected name - to about a dozen London sites.

restaurants.name: Nardulli
restaurants.whyGo: On Clapham Common and family-run, which in south London gelato is a very short list.

restaurants.name: Chin Chin
restaurants.whyGo: Ice cream frozen to order with liquid nitrogen - theatre as much as dessert, and it was doing it long before the format spread.

restaurants.name: Mamasons Dirty Ice Cream
restaurants.whyGo: Ube halaya ice cream in a squishy bun - Filipino sorbetes, and unlike anything else on a London ice cream list.

restaurants.name: The Connaught Bar
restaurants.whyGo: The martini is mixed at your table from a trolley of tinctures and you choose as it goes - twice voted the best bar in the world, and on the list more times than any other bar ever.
restaurants.signals: World's 50 Best Bars - twice number one

restaurants.name: Tayēr + Elementary
restaurants.whyGo: Alex Kratena and Monica Berg split it in two - a standing bar at the front, a seated tasting room behind - and it reached fourth in the world.
restaurants.signals: World's 50 Best Bars, 4th; Sustainable Bar of the Year

restaurants.name: Satan's Whiskers
restaurants.whyGo: No bookings, taxidermy on the walls, hip-hop loud enough to talk over, and a menu rewritten daily - named the best cocktail bar in London and third in the UK.
restaurants.opNote: Walk-in only, and it fills early. The menu changes every day.
restaurants.signals: UK Top 50 Cocktail Bars - best in London

restaurants.name: A Bar with Shapes for a Name
restaurants.whyGo: Built on Bauhaus principles down to the glassware, with a menu of about a dozen drinks and nothing surplus to it.

restaurants.name: Three Sheets
restaurants.whyGo: Two brothers, a short menu and no theatre - the drinks arrive without a speech, which in this scene is the point.

restaurants.name: Kwãnt
restaurants.whyGo: Erik Lorincz, formerly of the Savoy's American Bar, running a basement room under Shepherd Market.

restaurants.name: Scarfes Bar
restaurants.whyGo: Gerald Scarfe's caricatures cover the walls, there is a fire and a live band most nights, and it feels like a library that started serving drinks.

restaurants.name: Nightjar
restaurants.whyGo: Live jazz and blues every night in a basement off Old Street, with drinks built to match the era rather than the trend.
restaurants.opNote: Live music nightly, with a music charge after a certain hour. Book.

restaurants.name: The American Bar
restaurants.style: The oldest cocktail bar in London
restaurants.whyGo: Trading since the 1890s and the room where the Savoy Cocktail Book was written - a pianist, white jackets, and no concession to fashion.

restaurants.name: Artesian
restaurants.whyGo: Four consecutive years as the best bar in the world in the 2010s, and still a room built for a long drink rather than a quick one.

restaurants.name: Lyaness
restaurants.whyGo: Ryan Chetiyawardana builds the menu around a handful of house-made ingredients and rewrites it wholesale - a river view attached.

restaurants.name: Bar Termini
restaurants.whyGo: Twenty-odd seats, negronis aged in the bottle, and an espresso counter by day - closer to Rome than to Soho.

restaurants.name: Seed Library
restaurants.whyGo: Ryan Chetiyawardana again, in a stripped concrete basement doing short, low-alcohol drinks with none of the ceremony.

restaurants.name: Dukes Bar
restaurants.whyGo: The martini is made at your table from frozen bottles and there is a two-drink limit, which tells you most of what you need to know.
restaurants.opNote: A strict limit of two martinis per guest. It is not a suggestion.

restaurants.name: Swift
restaurants.whyGo: Quick drinks upstairs, a dark room and a long whisky list downstairs - built so you can use it either way.

restaurants.name: Coupette
restaurants.whyGo: Calvados and apple run through the whole menu - a bar with a thesis rather than a list.

restaurants.name: Happiness Forgets
restaurants.whyGo: Low ceilings, low light and a short menu under Hoxton Square - one of the rooms that started London's basement bar habit.

restaurants.name: Oriole
restaurants.whyGo: A basement off Smithfield market with live music nightly and a menu organised by continent - the sibling to Nightjar.

restaurants.name: Bar Crispin
restaurants.whyGo: A low-intervention list with food good enough that people book it as dinner rather than as drinks.

restaurants.name: Sager + Wilde
restaurants.whyGo: One of the rooms that made Hackney Road a wine destination, with a list that runs from cheap and interesting to seriously old.

restaurants.name: Diogenes the Dog
restaurants.whyGo: A small Elephant and Castle wine bar run by a master sommelier, which is not a sentence you get to write often.

restaurants.name: Half Cut Market
restaurants.whyGo: Buy a bottle off the shelf and drink it there for a small corkage - the format that makes a serious list affordable.

restaurants.name: Tayyabs
restaurants.whyGo: The sizzling lamb chops arrive still spitting and are the reason the queue forms - a Whitechapel institution since the 1970s that has never needed to change.
restaurants.opNote: BYOB, no bookings for small groups at peak, and loud. The queue is the system.

restaurants.name: Original Lahore Kebab House
restaurants.whyGo: Trading since 1972 on lamb chops, dry lamb curry and chicken karahi, in a room that has never pretended to be anything but a canteen.
restaurants.opNote: BYOB. Open late, which is half the reason it is busy.

restaurants.name: Namak Mandi
restaurants.whyGo: Peshawari cooking rather than Punjabi - namkeen karahi seasoned with salt and little else, which is a different tradition from everything else on this list.

restaurants.name: Lahori Nihaari
restaurants.whyGo: Built around nihari, the slow-cooked breakfast stew - a single-dish kitchen in a city with very few of them.

restaurants.name: Spice Village
restaurants.whyGo: A large, bright Tooting room built for families and big tables rather than for atmosphere.

restaurants.name: Salloos
restaurants.whyGo: A long-running family-run Knightsbridge room doing Pakistani cooking with tablecloths - almost the only one of its kind in London.

restaurants.name: Beigel Bake
restaurants.whyGo: Salt beef bagels around the clock on Brick Lane, sold through a hatch to a queue of people at every hour a person can be hungry.
restaurants.opNote: Open 24 hours, every day. The queue at 3am is a genuine London sight.

restaurants.name: Polo Bar
restaurants.whyGo: So committed to trading around the clock that it has no front door to close - a fry-up at any hour, beside Liverpool Street.
restaurants.opNote: Open 24 hours. There is literally no front door.

restaurants.name: Voodoo Ray's
restaurants.whyGo: Enormous New York slices sold until the small hours, which is the only specification that matters at that time of night.
restaurants.opNote: Serves well past midnight at weekends. Slices, not whole pizzas.

restaurants.name: Brick Lane Market
restaurants.whyGo: Vintage clothing, records and street food down the lane and through the Truman Brewery yards - the busiest and least curated of the east London Sunday markets.
restaurants.opNote: Sundays are the main event. The Truman Brewery yards run smaller markets on Saturdays too.

restaurants.name: The Holly Bush
restaurants.whyGo: A 1807 pub up an alley off Heath Street with panelled rooms, open fires and no through traffic - the most convincing surviving village pub in London.

restaurants.name: The Wells Tavern
restaurants.whyGo: The village's proper sit-down dinner pub, halfway between Hampstead and the Heath, and the one locals book for a occasion rather than a pint.

restaurants.name: Ginger & White
restaurants.whyGo: A small Perrins Court cafe doing serious coffee and a proper British breakfast, and the default Hampstead meeting place for anyone who lives there.
restaurants.signature: Bacon sandwich and a flat white

restaurants.name: Bonoo Indian Tapas
restaurants.whyGo: Indian small plates built on street food but cooked with British seasonal produce, and the one Hampstead room the local guides consistently put first.

restaurants.name: The Kitchen at Kenwood
restaurants.whyGo: In Kenwood's old brew house and service wing, with a terrace over the estate - the only proper stop on the northern half of the Heath.
restaurants.signature: Cake and a pot of tea on the terrace

restaurants.name: Parliament Hill Cafe
restaurants.whyGo: At the foot of the hill by the athletics track, and the obvious place to start or finish the climb to the Parliament Hill view.

restaurants.name: The Dysart
restaurants.whyGo: A Michelin star at the gates of Richmond Park, in an Arts and Crafts building, on a menu that changes with what Kenneth Culhane can actually get.

restaurants.name: Al Boccon di'vino
restaurants.whyGo: There is no menu. You are brought course after course of whatever is being cooked that night, the way an Italian wedding feeds people, until you stop.
restaurants.signature: Whatever arrives - you do not choose

restaurants.name: The White Cross
restaurants.whyGo: On the towpath where the river regularly comes over the road and floods the entrance - there are tide tables on the wall and wellingtons by the door.
restaurants.signature: A pint on the river wall at high tide

restaurants.name: Pembroke Lodge
restaurants.whyGo: A Georgian mansion inside Richmond Park with terraced gardens and, from King Henry's Mound just behind it, the protected ten-mile sightline to St Paul's.

restaurants.name: The Roebuck
restaurants.whyGo: Directly opposite the protected view from Richmond Hill - people buy a pint and carry it across the road to the wall, which is the accepted way to do it.
restaurants.signature: A pint taken across to the Terrace wall

restaurants.name: Antipodea
restaurants.whyGo: All-day Australian cooking that runs from brunch through laksa and Thai squid, which is a far broader range than Richmond's pub-and-Italian default.

restaurants.name: Barge East
restaurants.style: Seasonal British on a Dutch barge
restaurants.whyGo: A 1985 Dutch barge sailed over and permanently moored on the River Lea, with a garden alongside it and the Olympic Park skyline behind.

restaurants.name: CRATE Brewery
restaurants.whyGo: Hackney Wick's first craft brewery, in a former print factory on the canal, making the beer and the pizza in the same building.
restaurants.signature: Pizza and a pint on the towpath

restaurants.name: Bread Street Kitchen Stratford
restaurants.whyGo: The most serious kitchen at the gateway to Westfield, and the one place here that works for a proper dinner rather than a shopping break.

restaurants.name: Santi
restaurants.whyGo: East Village's own Italian rather than a Westfield unit, doing pizza and pasta for the people who actually live in the athletes' village.

restaurants.name: Bamboo Mat
restaurants.whyGo: Nikkei cooking - the Japanese-Peruvian tradition - which is a genuinely unexpected thing to find in Stratford and the reason to skip the chains.

restaurants.name: Kateh
restaurants.whyGo: A Michelin Bib Gourmand Persian kitchen in a small townhouse off Warwick Avenue, hung with Persian art and run more like a home than a restaurant.

restaurants.name: The Waterway
restaurants.whyGo: One of the largest canal-side terraces in London, right on the water at Little Venice, and the first thing in the area to fill up on a warm weekend.

restaurants.name: The Summerhouse
restaurants.whyGo: A New England-looking clapboard room right at the water's edge, doing seafood and fish and chips with the canal a metre from the table.
restaurants.signature: Fish and chips by the water

restaurants.name: Beany Green Little Venice
restaurants.whyGo: Australian brunch on the towpath with a big canal-side terrace, and the easiest good breakfast within walking distance of Paddington station.
restaurants.signature: Smashed avocado and a flat white

restaurants.name: The Town of Ramsgate
restaurants.whyGo: A pub on this spot since at least 1545, long and narrow, opening onto a small river terrace beside Wapping Old Stairs and Execution Dock.
restaurants.signature: A pint on the river terrace

restaurants.name: The Captain Kidd
restaurants.whyGo: A converted warehouse laid out like a ship's hull, named for the pirate hanged a few yards away, with the biggest river terrace in Wapping.
restaurants.signature: A pint on the Thames terrace

restaurants.name: Turner's Old Star
restaurants.whyGo: An 1830 back-street local that JMW Turner is said to have owned and run for a mistress - the last plain, unrenovated pub left in Wapping.
restaurants.signature: A quiet pint away from the river crowds

restaurants.name: Toulouse Lautrec
restaurants.style: French brasserie with a jazz club upstairs
restaurants.whyGo: Three floors of a converted pub run by three brothers since 2008: a rustic French brasserie at street level, a piano bar above it, and a proper jazz club on top for the weekend bands - South London's closest answer to a Soho jazz supper club, at Kennington prices.
restaurants.opNote: Live music most nights; club shows are ticketed separately from dinner (usually £10-20), so book the table and the show together. Piano bar sets are typically free.

restaurants.name: The Bull's Head
restaurants.style: Riverside gastropub with a dedicated jazz room
restaurants.whyGo: A jazz venue since 1959 - the same year Ronnie Scott's opened - and once nicknamed the suburban Ronnie Scott's: Coleman Hawkins, Ben Webster and Stan Tracey all played the back room, and a young Mick Jagger appeared here too. The music room still runs seven nights a week behind a working Young's gastropub on the Thames towpath.
restaurants.opNote: Music room seats around 70 and is ticketed separately from the pub; the dining rooms and riverside bar are normal pub service. Check the gig listing before travelling - the room is the point.

restaurants.name: The Montpelier
restaurants.whyGo: A Peckham corner local where the Sunday roast comes with a live jazz trio from 7.30pm - the current kitchen residency (Rocco) grills whole fish and shucks some of the better oysters in South London the rest of the week.
restaurants.opNote: Jazz is SUNDAYS ONLY, from 7.30pm - the rest of the week is quiz nights and DJs. The kitchen is a residency and changes hands, so check who is cooking before recommending the food specifically.

restaurants.name: Dishoom
restaurants.whyGo: The Irani cafes of old Bombay recreated in careful detail, and the bacon naan roll that made it a breakfast destination as much as a dinner one.
restaurants.opNote: Any party size can book before 6pm; after 6pm bookings are for groups of six or more only. Most tables are held back for walk-ins either way. Seven London branches; the Branches tab has six named.
